The motorcycle comes to rest a hundred feet down the road, lying on its side, still ticking as the engine cools. Its fairing has burst into confetti—red plastic shards scattered across two lanes, glinting in the sun like fallen leaves. One mirror stands upright in the gravel, still bolted to its stalk, reflecting a patch of sky the rider can't see. The front wheel has folded back against the frame at an angle wheels were never meant to hold. Coolant drips from a ruptured line, bright green, spreading into a pool of gasoline that throws faint rainbow circles across the asphalt. Behind it all, a long black scar of rubber marks where the rear tire fought the pavement, ending in a gouge where metal met road and lost.

Then—nothing. The roar that preceded all this is gone so completely it feels less like sound ending and more like sound never having existed. There is only ringing, high and thin, the ears' own damage humming in the vacuum. Slowly the world leaks back in: the tick of cooling metal. Liquid finding low places. Wind moving through roadside grass. A bird, somewhere, indifferent. The silence isn't peaceful—it's held breath, the whole scene suspended between the violence just past and whatever comes next.

The rider is twenty feet beyond the bike, having left it mid-air. He's conscious—that particular misfortune—flat on his back, staring straight up.

His leathers did what they could. Where they held, bruising blooms dark beneath the armor. Where they tore, the asphalt took payment. His left forearm is stripped to a raw expanse of weeping red—not bleeding so much as seeping, the way abrasions do, blood diluted with something clearer. Grit is embedded in it, tiny black stones pressed into the wound like shrapnel, along with threads of denim fused into the rawness by friction heat. His knee is worse: the jean leg shredded away entirely, the skin above it ground down past pink into a glistening, mottled depth that will take surgeons hours to clean. Road rash isn't a cut. It's sandpaper work—abrasion layered over burn—and every nerve in those exposed strips is reporting at once.

His right leg is simply wrong. Below the knee it angles outward where it should continue down, the boot toe pointing at the sky while his kneecap points ahead. The shinbone hasn't broken skin—not quite—but it presses against the inside of it, a pale ridge straining beneath flesh already swelling taut. His collarbone is a lump that shouldn't exist, tenting the shoulder of his jacket. When he tries to move that arm, the signal travels as far as the shoulder and dies there, replaced by a white flash that makes his vision swim.

Shock arrives quietly now, doing him a strange favor. Cold spreads through him despite the warm afternoon. His teeth begin to chatter. The pain comes in waves, each one slightly delayed, as though his body is opening envelopes one at a time instead of reading them all at once. He hears his own breathing—fast, shallow, whistling through a mouth that tastes of copper and asphalt.

Then, far off: tires on pavement, slowing. A door. Footsteps beginning to run.

# Full Moon Road

Mara heard the second set of footsteps before she saw anything at all.

She'd been walking the two miles home from the diner the way she always did—down Mill Road, past the shuttered feed store, into the stretch where the trees leaned over the asphalt and swallowed the streetlight glow. Eleven forty on a Tuesday night in October. Her breath came out in little ghosts. Her keys were threaded between her fingers, a habit her mother had drilled into her.

But now there was another rhythm underneath her own. Slightly heavier. Slightly slower. *Crunch. Crunch.* Gravel and frost.

She stopped.

It stopped.

An echo, she told herself. Just an echo off the tree line. She walked faster, and the sound kept pace, patient, unhurried, until she broke into a jog and it did too—and then the jog became a run, and the run became a sprint, and she burst out of the tunnel of trees into the open field by the old water tower, lungs burning—

And it stepped out of the treeline ahead of her.

A man. That was her first thought, absurdly: *a man*, naked in the freezing dark, standing forty feet away under the fat white moon. He was hunched forward, arms hanging too long, head tilted at an angle that made her stomach drop. He wasn't breathing hard. He'd been watching her the whole way.

"No," Mara whispered. "No no no—"

He took one step toward her, and then he made a sound—a small, wet *pop*, like a knuckle cracking somewhere deep inside his chest—and folded to his knees.

What happened next, she would never be able to fully describe, not if she lived a hundred years. She could only replay it in fragments.

His spine went first. She watched it bow, arch, *bend the wrong way*, and heard the vertebrae let go one after another—a rippling series of cracks running up his back like someone snapping green branches, each report louder than the last. His shoulders dislocated with a sound like wet rope tearing, the shoulder blades sliding visibly beneath the skin, migrating, reshaping. He screamed through all of it. That was the worst part, early on—that it was still a human scream, high and ragged and terrified, as though some part of him were awake in there, feeling every second.

Then his arms began to grow.

The forearms stretched, skin pulling taut and shiny, veins standing out like cords—and then the skin split. Not all at once. In seams. Thin lines opening along his forearms and shoulders, and through them pushed coarse black fur, dense and glistening, as if the hair had been waiting underneath all along. His hands hit the frost-covered grass and his fingers *lengthened*, joints popping in sequence down each one, nails thickening, darkening, curving over into yellow hooks that sank into the dirt.

His legs broke next. She heard the femurs snap—actually *snap*, sharp as rifle shots—and watched his shins reconfigure, the joints reversing, heels lifting off the ground until he stood on what looked like the backs of his feet. His whole frame lurched upward, taller, broader, his ribs audibly expanding outward like a cage being pried open. His clothes were gone—shredded, absorbed, irrelevant.

The screaming changed halfway through. It dropped in pitch, roughened, curdled into something between a roar and a howl, and by the time his jaw began to push outward—muzzle sliding free of his face in a grinding slide of bone, gums bleeding around a double row of teeth erupting through the flesh—he wasn't screaming words anymore. He wasn't screaming anything human at all.

Steam rose off him in the cold air. The smell reached her where she stood rooted to the spot: copper and musk and something like a wet animal in summer, thick enough to taste.

And then it was done.

The thing that rose to its full height in the moonlight was seven feet of black-furred muscle, chest heaving, head lowered between massive shoulders. It shook itself once, a violent ripple from ears to tail, and droplets of sweat flew off it like sparks.

Mara's legs finally remembered how to work. She stumbled backward, one step, two, her heel catching on frozen ground.

The creature's head swung toward her.

Its eyes caught the moon and held it—amber, luminous, and horribly *aware*. Not the blank shine of a beast. Something looked out of those eyes. Something that knew exactly what she was seeing, and exactly what she was thinking, and exactly which direction she would run.

It took a single step toward her. Deliberate. Unhurried. The clawed foot pressed into the frost without a sound.

Mara turned and ran.

The patient is a dockworker, thirty years old, his left leg shattered below the knee by a falling crate. He has been given a dram of gin and a dose of laudanum, and neither will be nearly enough. Four porters pin him to the table—one across each arm, one on each shoulder—because no strap ever devised can contain what a human body does when the knife goes in.

There is no time for kindness. In this era, mercy is measured in seconds. A surgeon's fame rests entirely on his speed; the great operators are discussed the way racehorses are, and the fastest men can take off a leg in under three minutes, first cut to final stitch. Slowness kills. Every extra moment on the table is a step closer to shock and collapse.

A leather tourniquet is cinched above the knee and screwed tight until the limb turns pale and bloodless. The surgeon takes up his catlin—a long, straight amputation knife—and does not pause. One stroke carries the blade in a complete circle around the calf, parting skin like wet paper. A second stroke, deeper, hews through the muscle to the bone. The scream arrives with the very first cut—not a word, not a cry, something older than language—a raw, rising shriek that cracks and renews itself as breath allows. His back bows off the table. The porters throw their whole weight onto him.

With the muscle flaps dragged aside by retractors, the bone stands bare and white. The saw crosses the tibia in perhaps ten strokes, a grinding rasp the patient feels in his teeth—and then the leg is free, lifted away and dropped into a bucket at the surgeon's feet. Now comes the worst of it. The tourniquet is eased, and the severed femoral artery erupts. Bright arterial blood leaps six, eight inches, pulsing in rhythm with the racing heart, spattering the surgeon's cuffs, his assistants' aprons, the upturned faces of students in the gallery above. Hands dart in with forceps and ligatures, chasing the spurt, tying it off. A cautery iron hisses against the smaller vessels. Blood runs between the floorboards into the sawdust scattered there for precisely this purpose.

Knife to last ligature: ninety seconds. The stump is bound, and the man—grey-lipped, soaked, his voice worn down to a hoarse animal moaning—is carried to a ward, where his odds of surviving the week hover near fifty-fifty. Hospital gangrene will claim many who live past the table. The surgeon peels off his sodden apron, wipes the blade on his sleeve, and calls for the next patient. There are eleven more on the list.

It is 1841. Ether is five years away. When it finally arrives, older surgeons are said to have wept—not with joy, but with grief for every patient who had gone before.

# The Last of Him

The fever took Elias's voice first, and then, hour by hour, everything else—the color in his lips, the steadiness of his hands, the jokes he kept making anyway, thinner each time, like a signal fading on a radio nobody would turn off.

They had been arguing for two hours, in whispers, as if the thing in the trees could hear doubt.

Dana knelt at the washbasin, scrubbing the bite on his forearm with the last of the alcohol. Third time that day. The wound didn't bleed anymore. It wept—a thin gray seep no bandage stayed dry against. She scrubbed like the infection were a stain, like elbow grease had jurisdiction here.

"Fevers break," she said, to no one, to everyone. "I've seen fevers break."

"You've seen people die," Hollis said from the window. He sat with the knife across his knees, watching the treeline. "Everyone here has. Say it plain, Dana. It's kinder."

"I knew a man in Harlow who—"

# The Margin

He was fine for eleven days.

That was the part no one warned you about — not the guilt, not the fear, but the ease. He slept. He ate eggs. He went back to work on Monday, shook hands, asked after a colleague's daughter, laughed at a joke at the right moment. The story he had built — an argument, an accident, a man who fell — sat in his mouth like a smooth stone, worn round by rehearsal. And the world accepted it. That was the vertigo: not that he might be caught, but that he wasn't. That the world had looked at him and seen nothing worth looking at. He had killed a man, and the universe had not so much as changed the weather.

The fourteenth day, he saw him in the hallway.

Or: the shape of him. Standing where the kitchen light gave out, at the seam between light and dark, weight on one hip the way he always stood, head tipped as if waiting for a sentence to finish. He turned. Nothing, of course. A coat on a hook he'd stopped seeing months ago. He stood there a long time, heart going like a fist on a door.

He learned the rules quickly, the way the body learns to flinch. Don't look directly. Direct looking was a door that closed. The man existed only in the margin — that thin, unreliable crescent at the edge of sight — and so he learned to live with his head slightly turned, forever catching, never catching. He rearranged the apartment around it. He stopped walking the long hallway. He ate facing the wall. The house became a diagram of angles, and he was the only one who could read it.

Then the details started.

That was worse. A shape could be fatigue; a shape could be the eye's old habit of making men out of shadow. But the shape wore the gray cardigan with the missing button at the cuff. The shape *leaned*. And one evening, standing at the sink, he caught it — three notes, hummed low, always the same three notes, the man's thinking-sound, the sound he'd made over crossword puzzles and unpaid invoices — coming out of his own mouth.

He spat the water and stood shaking. The dead don't need to speak, he understood then. They need only be recognized.

He had stopped using the man's name weeks ago, even inside his own head. A name was a handle. He could no longer afford to hold on.

The story he'd built began to rot from the inside. For the first week it had been self-defense. By the second week, necessity. By the third, he had stopped naming it at all, which was its own confession. And his memory — his memory was worse than disloyal; it was *creative*. In the new version, the man had stepped closer first. Had raised his voice first. Had said the thing, the unforgivable thing — though he could no longer find the thing anywhere, only the certainty that it had been said. Memory was revising itself to save him, sanding the night smooth. And the man in the corner of his eye stood exactly the way he had stood that night, and looked at him exactly the way he had looked — patient, archival, refusing the revision. The ghost was not haunting him. The ghost was testifying.

His body went next. Sleep came in shallow pieces, if at all; he lay listening to the apartment's vocabulary of creaks, sorting each one into *man* or *house*, and the sorting never finished. Food tasted of copper, or of nothing. He stopped shaving, because mirrors had become windows he didn't control — and once, only once, his reflection turned its head a half-second after he did. He told no one. Telling would make it a thing in the world, and things in the world could be examined. This had to stay a thing in the angle, where it couldn't be caught.

He moved in the spring. New city, third floor, no history. He stood in the empty living room with his boxes and felt, for one clean hour, the silence of a man who might still be saved. Then, unpacking, he saw it: the shape at the edge of the doorway. Cardigan. Hip cocked. Head tipped. And he understood — with the flat, falling feeling of a diagnosis — that it had never been the house. Never the light, or the hallway, or his eyes. It was in him. He had not brought the man with him. He had become the room the man stood in.

After that, he stopped fighting, and this was the rot's true genius: the fighting had been the last of him. He left the corner by the window empty. He stopped sitting in the chair that faced the doorway. He began, without ever deciding to, to narrate his day aloud — not to himself; he was past self-address — to the margin. "They were out of the coffee you liked," he said one evening, and heard his own voice in the silence, and the silence did not answer, and he understood that it never would. That this was the cruelest architecture of all: guilt does not want revenge. Guilt wants nothing. It only stands where you put it and waits for you to keep talking.

Then came the face. He was shaving — he had started shaving again, some last instinct toward the human — when he realized he could no longer call the man's face to mind. Head-on, it was gone. Memory had taken even that, had sanded it away with everything else. The only place the face still existed was the corner of his eye. The dead man was now more real to him than his own reflection — more detailed, more constant, more *present*. He began turning faster and faster, trying to surprise it. He set two mirrors facing each other to trap it in the corridor between them. He stood in corners himself for hours, trying to see what the man saw.

The last night, he decided to face it. He turned, slowly, deliberately, all the way around, and gave the corner the full weight of his gaze — the look he had never once given the man while he was alive.

Nothing. A wall. A shadow that was only a shadow. Eleven months, and the man was gone — and he sat down on the floor and wept, not from relief, because there was no relief. He had killed him once in the world and once in memory, and now this — the last of him, gone too. The haunting had been the only place the man still lived. And he had looked at it directly. And looking was a door that closed.

The neighbors hear him through the wall some evenings. He talks to someone, they say — to the corner, they think. His voice is gentle. It is the voice of a man who has finally learned to listen. And it never stops, because every room he will ever stand in has a corner, and the corner is always there, and he has nothing left now but to keep the conversation going for both of them.

His ankles were strapped higher than his head. Blood pooled behind his eyes. The ceiling light hung above him like a pale moon he was falling away from.

"You know how this goes," one of them said. He couldn't tell their voices apart anymore. Three days, or four. "You breathe when we let you breathe."

The cloth came down over his face. Thin cotton, dry at first, smelling of bleach. It clung to the hollows of his cheeks, dipped into the wells of his nostrils. He told himself: *it's just cloth. It's nothing. You can still breathe.*

Cold—colder than he expected, cold as a river in March—and it did not run off him. It soaked the cloth and the cloth sealed itself against his skin, and suddenly there was no air anywhere in the world. Not in the room. Not in his chest. Nowhere.

His body knew before his mind did. His throat slammed shut—a hard, involuntary clamp, the body's ancient answer to water, the same reflex that keeps a newborn from drowning in its first bath. Except now the reflex was trapping him. He tried to open his throat and it would not open. He tried to breathe and there was nothing to breathe.

He held his breath. That was the mistake, though no one had ever taught him otherwise. Holding felt like safety. Holding was what you did underwater. But he wasn't underwater—he was on dry land, on a table, in a room where men stood calmly beside a bucket—and holding meant the fire started sooner.

It began in the center of his chest. A slow bloom of heat, then a clawing. His diaphragm spasmed, hauling upward again and again, trying to drag air through a sealed door. His ribs ached. Somewhere far away he heard a sound like an animal in a snare and understood dimly that it was coming out of him.

*Count,* he told himself. *Count the seconds.* One. Two. Three—

He lost the numbers. Panic ate them. That was the thing no one warned you about: drowning wasn't peaceful, wasn't the quiet blue drift people described. Drowning was a riot. Every nerve in his body screamed the same single word—*breathe*—and every instinct demanded he fight, and he fought, wrenching against the straps hard enough to tear skin, heels drumming the steel, back bowing off the table. The restraints didn't budge. Nothing budged. The water kept coming, patient as rain.

He would have told them anything. He understood that now, in the last bright second before his mind went white at the edges. Not because he was weak—because the body does not negotiate. The body only knows it is dying, and it will trade everything, every name, every secret, every friend, for one breath. He felt his mouth opening beneath the cloth, shaping words no one could hear, confessing to things he hadn't done, offering things he didn't have.

The water stopped.

The cloth peeled away and air hit his throat like a slap and he dragged it in—huge, ragged, whooping gulps—coughing until he tasted bile, until his eyes streamed. The room swam. The pale light overhead. The bucket, half empty. A man's shoes, perfectly dry, standing a polite distance away.

"There," someone said, almost gently. "Now. The names of your unit."

He breathed. He breathed because he could, because each breath was a miracle and a humiliation. And he knew—with the terrible clarity of a man hanging off a cliff—that in thirty seconds, maybe less, they would lift the bucket again, and he would say whatever they wanted, and afterward he would have to live inside what he'd said. If he lived at all.

The cloth descended. He was already begging. He heard himself and did not recognize his own voice.

She'd been running long enough that the running had become the whole world: the slap of her boots, the fire in her lungs, and beneath it all that sound she refused to listen to—the soft, rhythmic patter of paws in powder. Many of them. Keeping pace without effort.

The trees thinned without her noticing, and then they simply gave up. Nothing ahead but a granite face rising out of the drifts, sheer and blue-gray and absolute. Later she would understand they hadn't followed her here by accident. They'd herded her, the way water herds a leaf.

She spun with her back against the stone, breath tearing out of her in white rags. They came out of the treeline at a walk. Five of them, maybe six—the snow-light made them flicker, gray shapes resolving and dissolving at the edges of her vision. None of them were panting anymore. She was the only thing in the clearing making noise.

The big one stepped forward, head low, and she snatched up a broken branch and swung it, screaming—and the wolf flowed back from the arc of it like water.

The world exploded against the back of her leg.

That was the strange part, the part she'd keep returning to: there was no pain. Not at first. The cold had been working on her for hours, had long since drawn a white curtain over everything below her knees, and so the first bite arrived as pure *force*—a weight slamming into her, pressure like a door closing on her flesh—and she was already falling when her body finally translated it. Teeth. Teeth, deep in the muscle above her knee.

Then the heat.

It poured down her calf scalding and obscene, because her skin had forgotten what warm was. Hours of wind and snow had cooled her to the temperature of the world around her, and now her own blood—her own heat, ninety-eight degrees of it—ran over skin gone the color of the sky, and it *burned*. Genuinely burned. Steam rose off her leg, a thin ghost of vapor curling up from the wound into air far colder than she was, and some traitorous animal part of her brain registered the warmth as relief, as mercy, wanted to press herself deeper into it—

Then the pain arrived, late and total, white-hot where the heat had been red.

The wolf shook its head, worrying the wound the way a dog worries a rope, and she went down into the snow. It was soft. It was everywhere. It drank the blood almost instantly, each drop landing with a small dark kiss and blooming outward, red soaking into white, melting little craters that refroze at their edges. She could see it upside-down between her own boots and thought, absurdly: *it looks like berries.*

Her hands were too cold to feel the snow they grabbed. Her leg was on fire. Caught between those two facts, her body could no longer tell which end of her was real.

---

# Conduction

The rain over Sector Nine fell in slow, greasy sheets, each drop catching the amber glow of the ad-veins crawling up the hab-towers. Ilse Varga stood beneath a noodle stall's awning, collar up, watching the crowd thin out around the transit plaza. Her retinal overlay painted the world in soft telemetry: heat blooms, gait signatures, the faint gold thread of a stolen ident-chip moving through the crowd at 1.4 meters per second.

There. Dennick Roan. Former corporate enforcer, current data smuggler, current problem. His face was three weeks of bad decisions wrapped around a jaw that had been broken twice and set once.

Ilse moved.

Roan felt her before he saw her—bounty hunters have a smell, he'd told people once, half-joking—and he broke into a run, shoulder-checking a fruit vendor into his own cart. Mangos skittered across wet pavement. The crowd shrieked and parted, and Roan went through the gap like water through a cracked dam, vaulting a barricade, cutting down the maintenance alley behind the plaza where the light didn't reach.

Ilse didn't sprint. She tracked. Her boots found the same gaps in the crowd, her overlay holding his gold thread even as he ducked under a steam vent and scrambled up a service ladder toward the maglev platform overhead. She unclipped the weapon from her hip as she walked: the VK-7 "Lodestar," a compact arc projector with two hair-thin filament darts and a power cell that hummed against her palm like a sleeping insect.

At the top of the ladder, Roan hauled himself onto the platform and turned, breathing hard, a ceramic knife already out of his sleeve. Below, the hunter stepped into the alley's mouth, unhurried, rain beading on her shoulders.

"Contract says alive," she called up. "Doesn't say *comfortable*. Your call."

Roan answered by throwing the knife.

It was a good throw—she'd give him that—but she'd watched his shoulder load up a half-second early, and she was already sidestepping when it hissed past her ear and buried itself in a drainage pipe. In the same motion she raised the Lodestar and fired.

The darts crossed eight meters of rainy air in a blink and bit through his jacket, one above the collarbone, one into the meat of his thigh. A microsecond later, the filaments went live.

Fifty thousand volts surged down the wires—not enough *current* to stop a heart, but far more than enough voltage to punch through skin, fabric, and air gap alike, delivering a few milliamps of precisely shaped charge straight into the machinery of his nervous system. The Lodestar's waveform cycled at nineteen pulses per second, each one a small, arrogant shout that drowned out everything else his body was trying to say.

His brain issued the order: *run.* His body never heard it. The current had seized the line.

Every skeletal muscle between the two darts fired at once—not smoothly, but in the ragged, synchronized convulsions of tissue being driven by a signal it couldn't refuse. His legs locked rigid, then buckled. His arms drew inward, fists clenching hard enough that the nails carved crescents into his palms. His core spasmed and folded him at the waist, and he dropped to the platform deck in a heap that made a sound like a dropped bag of tools.

Inside him, the chaos compounded. Motor neurons that should have whispered were screaming. His diaphragm stuttered mid-breath, leaving him gasping in shallow, useless sips of air. Pain receptors lit up along every nerve path the current touched—a white-hot, buzzing agony concentrated at the two dart sites, radiating outward until his whole body felt like one raw, singing wire. Somewhere beneath it, his muscles were burning through their energy reserves, flooding themselves with lactic acid, mortgaging tomorrow's strength to pay tonight's debt.

The Lodestar's designers had spent decades tuning the pulse shape so the current would pass *around* the heart rather than through its rhythm—safe enough to be street-legal, cruel enough to end a fight. Five seconds was all the law allowed. It was four seconds more than anyone needed.

The cycle ended. The filaments retracted with a soft pneumatic sigh.

Roan lay on the deck, twitching in diminishing aftershocks, chest heaving, sweat and rain mixing on his gray face. He tried to push himself up and got one elbow under him before his arm simply declined the instruction, trembling, spent. His mind was a smear of static—disoriented, slow, the world arriving a beat late. Every muscle group the current had commandeered now reported in with a deep, bruised ache, the dull fire of sustained contraction.

Ilse climbed the ladder, stepped over him, and cinched flex-cuffs around his wrists with practiced efficiency. Then, because the contract said *alive* and because she wasn't a monster, she pressed two fingers to his throat. Pulse elevated but steady. Breathing ragged but present. The little red welts at the dart sites would sting for days; the soreness would linger longer.

"You threw a knife at me," she said, hauling him into a sitting position against a support strut.

Roan's jaw worked. What came out was mostly a rasp. "...worth a try."

"It really wasn't." She keyed her wrist-comm. "Varga. Package secured. Send the skiff."

She stood there in the rain while they waited, watching the ad-veins crawl their endless amber loops up the towers, listening to the man behind her breathe—shallow, shaky, human. The Lodestar went back on her hip, humming its quiet insect hum, patient as weather.

In Sector Nine, everyone conducted something. Currents, contraband, other people's debts.

Ilse just tried to make sure hers never killed anybody.

# First, Do No Harm

Mara Voss woke to the smell of a hospital that had died.

Antiseptic, yes — but underneath it something older, ferrous, like blood that had soaked into grout decades ago and never left. Cold tile pressed against her cheek. A fluorescent tube buzzed somewhere above, cycling through a frequency that made her molars ache.

She knew hospitals the way priests know cathedrals. This one was wrong.

The weight registered next. Her left arm was extended across a steel table, wrist locked in a machined cradle, fingers spread and pinned beneath five small hinged plates — little steel lids, like the doors of reliquaries. Above her forearm hung an articulated arm bearing a broad surgical blade, angled with terrible patience. Beside it, a red readout burned: **03:00**, and already falling.

Before she was fully awake, before thought, her body did what bodies do: her right hand found her thigh and dug in, nails through cloth, a small bright sting. Proof of consciousness. Later she would remember that — the day's first wound, self-administered, a courtesy compared to what the room had planned.

A dictaphone clicked alive, zip-tied to the table leg.

> *"Good morning, Doctor. Guilt keeps its own clock, so I won't ask the time. Three years ago you stood over Elliot Reyes with wine under your mask and your hands unsteady, and he died believing he was safe. You wrote 'unforeseen complication.' You kept your license. You kept your hands.*
>
> *Today we address the ledger. The middle plate is latched from beneath. No tool opens it from above — the latch answers only to pressure from within, and only the finger itself can provide that pressure. Press down, and the plate will open. What remains of the finger is the fee. The lock accepts one currency.*
>
> *The blade above does not negotiate. Three minutes. Live or die, Doctor — the choice, as ever, is in your hands."*

The tape ended. Somewhere in the walls, hydraulics sighed, and the blade began its descent.

---

Denial came first, as it always does. She pulled against the cradle until the skin of her wrist rasped raw against steel. She pried at the middle plate with her right hand's fingernails, broke two of them, achieved nothing. She screamed, and the soundproofed tiles drank it whole. She found the camera then — a black eye in the ceiling corner — and spoke to it in a voice that started as negotiation and ended as prayer. *I'll confess. I'll sign anything. I'll stand up in front of the board and say his name.*

Silence. **02:31.**

Rage came after — heels hammering the table, curses spat at the lens — and rage burned fast, leaving only trembling. And in the space the trembling opened, the memories got in. The monitor's tone flattening to a single note she still heard in the shower sometimes. The word *complication* in her own handwriting. At the funeral, the widow had shaken her hand gently, and the gentleness had been worse than any slap.

Then the strangest thing: her left hand began to feel like an object. A thing bolted to the end of her arm. She caught herself addressing it silently — *you* — apologizing to it. Some older part of her brain, the part that had watched her drink three glasses of chardonnay before a nine-hour case, was trying to amputate her attachment ahead of schedule.

And beneath all of it ran the seduction she was most ashamed of: *let it take the arm.* The blade would descend, and it would be over, and none of it would be her doing. Blamelessness. The sweetest drug she'd ever been offered. She could freeze, and the harm would belong entirely to the room.

**02:04.**

She thought of Elliot Reyes again, and this time she made herself hold the thought. Every falsified chart was a sentence written in a language of harm. Here, at last, was a chance to enter something true into the record.

She stopped fighting the room and began preparing for it — because that was the one skill she had never lost. Preparation.

---

She inventoried like a surgeon before an incision. On a small steel tray beside the table: gauze, surgical tape, a rolled leather strap. Placed there before she'd woken. The room expected her to survive. Somehow that was worse than the blade.

# The Plank

The *Serpent's Kiss* rolled gently on a dead-calm sea, her sails hanging slack as the crew gathered along the starboard rail. The sun hung low and orange on the horizon, painting the water in colors far too beautiful for what was about to happen.

Captain Elias Graves stood at the gangway, his weathered face unreadable beneath the brim of his hat. Before him, bound at the wrists, knelt Thomas Finch—the boatswain who had whispered poison into the crew's ears for three weeks before raising his blade against his captain in the dark of night.

"Thomas Finch," Graves said, his voice carrying across the silent deck. "You conspired against your captain. You put steel to my throat while I slept." He drew his cutlass slowly, letting the sound of steel leaving leather stretch into eternity. "By the articles we all signed, there is but one punishment."

Two sailors hauled Finch to his feet and dragged him toward the plank—a rough length of timber extending six feet beyond the hull, suspended over water so clear that every detail of the world below was visible.

And the world below was *occupied*.

Finch saw them first as shadows—three great shapes sliding beneath the surface, twenty feet down, then fifteen, then ten. As they rose, their forms resolved into nightmare: bull sharks, each longer than a rowboat, their gray bodies moving with terrible patience. One passed directly beneath the plank's end, and Finch could see its pale belly, the slow sweep of its tail, the black, expressionless eye that rolled upward as if taking his measure.

"No—" Finch's voice cracked. His legs buckled, and the sailors holding him had to lock their arms under his shoulders to keep him upright. "Captain, please. Ten years I've sailed with you. Ten years! I was mad with drink, I swear it—"

"You were mad with ambition," Graves said flatly. "There's a difference."

They forced him up onto the plank. It flexed under his boots, and he froze, arms pinwheeling, a whimper escaping him that he would have killed any man yesterday for hearing. The sea stretched out endless and glittering around him, and beneath his feet, close enough now that he could count the scars on its skin, a shark turned in a slow circle. Its dorsal fin broke the surface for a moment—a gray scythe tracing lazy arcs around the hull, patient as death itself.

"Walk," Graves said.

"I can't—I can't swim, Captain, the sharks—"

"The sharks are why you'll walk quick, then." There was no cruelty in the captain's voice, which somehow made it worse. Only the flat certainty of a man reading a ledger.

A shark bumped the hull. The whole ship felt it—a soft, grinding thud that traveled up through the timbers and into Finch's bones. He screamed then, high and raw, and began to move—not walking so much as stumbling forward in jerking steps, tears streaming down his salt-crusted face, whispering prayers to a God he'd never once thought of in fair weather.

Halfway down the plank, he stopped. Looked back. Looked down.

The largest shark had risen almost to the surface now, its fin slicing a white wake as it circled beneath him. Through the crystalline water, Finch watched its jaws part slightly, rows of teeth glinting like broken porcelain.

"Please," he whispered.

Graves raised his cutlass and pointed seaward.

Finch closed his eyes—and walked.

The splash was small. The silence afterward was not.

Mara felt it before she saw it: a weight against her sternum, dense and wrong, like someone had set a brick on her ribs while she slept. She looked down.

A gray metal box, the size of a paperback, sat strapped to her chest with wide bands of duct tape. The tape's edges had already begun to curl away from her skin, gummy and pale, and where it gripped she could feel every ridge of her own ribcage, every breath pressing her flesh up into the adhesive and peeling it back again. Someone had taped the thing directly to her bare skin.

Wires. Three of them—red, yellow, one striped black-and-white that kept catching the light—snaked out of the box's seam and looped around her shoulders like parasitic vines. When she moved, even slightly, she felt them shift against her collarbone, thin rubber skins stretched over copper veins. One had slipped beneath her tank top strap and lay in the hollow of her throat, warm now, warmed by her own body heat, which was somehow worse than if it had been cold.

And underneath it all, faint but insistent, a sound.

*Tick.*

She held her breath to listen. *Tick. Tick.* Small, dry, mechanical. A sound with no malice in it at all, which made it obscene. It came from inside the box, patient as a clock in a schoolroom.

"No," she said aloud, to no one. "No, no, no—"

Her hands rose without her permission. She caught them hovering an inch from the casing, trembling so hard the motion blurred. *Don't touch it. You don't touch it, that's in every movie*—but her fingers wanted to claw, wanted to dig under the tape and tear the whole thing off her body and hurl it through the window, and she had to press her palms flat against her thighs to keep them still. Even that made her flinch, because her thighs were shaking too. Everything was shaking. Her teeth chattered out a rhythm that tangled horribly with the tick.

*Tick.*

She tried to count the intervals. *One-Mississippi. Two-* But her heart was slamming so hard she could feel it knocking against the underside of the box—a second clock, a faster one—and she couldn't tell which beat was which anymore, whether the bomb was keeping time with her pulse or her pulse was racing to catch up to the bomb.

Her vision went grainy at the edges. The room tilted. She thought about the red wire. Everyone knew about the red wire. *Cut the red wire.* But two of the wires were reddish, and her hands were useless, wet, shaking things, and the tape was fused to her skin, and when she breathed too deeply the whole assembly *creaked*—a tiny plastic groan that stopped her heart entirely.

*Tick.*

A laugh climbed out of her, high and cracked, one syllable of it, and then it turned into something else, something wetter. Her legs resigned without consulting her, and she slid down the wall, freezing mid-fall, half-crouched, arms out, balanced like a woman playing statues over her own death.

*Tick. Tick.*

"Please," she whispered—to the empty apartment, to whoever had done this, to the box itself. "Please, please, please."

The word dissolved as she said it. *Please* became a sound became a breath became just air moving through the throat of a body that had a bomb for a heart.

*Tick.*

The storm killed the power at 11:47, and by midnight Mara had learned the true weight of the dark.

It wasn't like night. Night had edges—streetlight bleeding through curtains, the green blink of the smoke detector. This was total, a darkness with texture, and she moved through it with one hand on the wall, fingertips reading the house like braille: smooth plaster, the cold lip of a picture frame, the nub of a nailhead, then nothing where the hallway opened into the living room.

Two steps down. She knew it was two steps down.

She lifted her foot anyway, and her heel met empty air, and for one lurching second the whole world was falling—arms pinwheeling, stomach rising—before her toes slapped the lower floor and she caught herself against the doorframe, heart slamming.

"Okay," she whispered. "Okay, okay."

Somewhere ahead, the refrigerator hummed its thin mechanical note. She aimed for it. The kitchen meant the junk drawer, meant the heavy rubber flashlight she'd kept there since she moved in and never once needed. Pip had vanished under the bed hours ago and refused all negotiation, which should have told her something, but she wasn't thinking about the cat. She was thinking about the flashlight, and about how a house she'd lived in for four years became a stranger the instant the lights died.

Lightning strobed through the curtains.

For half a heartbeat the living room printed itself onto her eyes—couch, coffee table, the window with rain crawling down it in silver ropes—and in the corner, between the bookshelf and the wall, something else. An interruption in the dark that was darker than the dark around it.

Then white, then black again, and the corner was only a corner.

Coat rack, she told herself. The guitar case. Her own reflection in the glass of the framed photo.

The first warning is the smell — sharp, chemical, like bleach concentrated into something that bites. Then the cloud comes over the parapet, green-yellow, heavier than air, sliding down into the trench like something alive and hungry.

His first breath is a mistake he doesn't know he's making. It tastes of metal and acid. Within seconds his eyes are streaming — not tears but a scalding flood, the world smeared into watercolor. His throat closes around a fire. He fumbles for his mask with hands that no longer feel like his own, fingers gone clumsy, straps tangling, and the whole time he's holding his breath, cheeks ballooned, chest burning, because some animal part of him knows the next breath will hurt.

It does. It's like swallowing broken glass and hot coals at once. The gas finds the wet tissue of his airways and becomes acid there — in the throat, the bronchi, the delicate sacs of the lungs. He doubles over the duckboards, coughing — not a cough but a convulsion, his whole body jackknifing with each spasm until his ribs ache and something warm and coppery threads through the froth gathering at his lips.

Then comes the drowning. This is what the training pamphlets never explain: the gas doesn't kill like a poison. It kills like a river. His lungs begin to weep, flooding with fluid the body produces to defend itself and which drowns it instead. Each breath draws less air through more water. He can hear it — a wet gurgle, a rattle in his own chest — and all around him the same sound from other men, the trench filling with a chorus of wheezing and bubbling, men on their knees, men clawing at the earth walls trying to climb above the gas where it pools like fog at the bottom of a well.

The mind fractures along predictable lines. First denial — *it's smoke, it will pass, it can't be this.* Then the animal panic: he tears at his collar, his mask, his own throat. Time distorts; seconds stretch into minutes. He watches the man beside him go down and feels something for which *horror* is too clean a word. There is bargaining — prayers, promises, deals struck with a God who seems very far from the mud. And underneath it all, a strange, detached lucidity: he notices the color of the sky above the gas cloud, the cold mud between his fingers, absurd small things, because his mind is fleeing a pain too large to hold in one piece.

As the oxygen starves him, his lips turn blue, then gray. His vision tunnels and sparkles at the edges. Confusion sets in — he may forget where he is, try to walk somewhere, *anywhere*, away from an enemy that is already inside him. Some men go quiet at the end, eerily calm, a false peace as the brain begins to fail. Others fight until the last, clawing the trench wall, the whistling sound of air forcing itself through swollen, fluid-choked passages growing thinner and thinner.

If he survives — hauled upwind, lungs ravaged — the aftermath is its own country. Weeks of coughing up the wreckage of his own tissue. Weakness so profound that stairs become mountains. Nightmares of drowning on dry land, night after night. And a permanent wound written into the senses: the flinch at any sharp chemical smell, the way bleach or chlorine — a swimming pool, a cleaned floor — will drop him back into that trench in an instant, chest tightening around a fire that exists now only in memory, and in the body that refuses to forget it.

**INT. BACK ROOM OF LUCIA'S RESTAURANT — NIGHT**

*The room smells of espresso and cigar smoke. SALVATORE "SAL" MORETTI, 60s, silver-haired, immaculate, sits behind a desk too big for the space. Across from him, ROCCO, 40s, stands with his hat in his hands.*

**ROCCO**
It's confirmed. Three meetings with the federal people. He wore a wire to the second one.

*Sal doesn't look up. He peels an orange in one long, unbroken spiral.*

**SAL**
A wire. In my house.

**ROCCO**
Since spring, maybe longer.

*A long silence. Sal sets the orange down and wipes his hands on a linen napkin, fold by fold.*

**SAL**
Tommy poured the wine at my daughter's wedding. Held my grandson at his christening. You know what the shame of it is? He was good. Never missed a payment. Never missed a Sunday dinner.

**ROCCO**
What do you want done?

**SAL**
Nothing dramatic. Nothing loud. Look at the man lately — the stress is eating him alive. You can see it in his face. What Tommy needs now is rest. A long rest. Somewhere quiet, where no one can reach him.

**ROCCO**
And if he doesn't come quietly?

**SAL**
Then help him relax.

*Rocco nods slowly.*

**SAL (CONT'D)**
No mess. And not near his mother's house — she's buried enough this year. When it's finished, settle his accounts, square things with his wife. Send flowers to the wake. White lilies.

**ROCCO**
White lilies.

**SAL**
He liked them. Funny, isn't it. After all this, I still remember what the man liked.

*He resumes peeling the orange.*

**SAL (CONT'D)**
His brother works the fish market. The brother touches nothing, knows nothing. He stays untouched. We're not animals.

**ROCCO**
Understood.

**SAL**
One thing more. Before the end, you sit with him. You tell him the boss remembers when they were family, and that he's sorry it came to this. Then you do what must be done.

*Rocco puts on his hat.*

**ROCCO**
It'll be handled tonight.

**SAL**
*(finally looking up)*
"Handled" is what you do with paperwork. The man gets his dignity. Say it properly.

**ROCCO**
*(a beat)*
...It'll be taken care of.

**SAL**
There it is.

*Rocco exits. Alone, Sal separates the orange into segments and eats one, unhurried. From the dining room, faintly, an old aria plays on the house speakers.*

**FADE OUT.**

The first shovelful landed like a dropped sandbag.

Then another. Another. The sound came through the lid muffled and dull—*thud, thud, thud*—a heartbeat played on a drum of pine. She lay still at first, hands folded where they'd been arranged, because some animal part of her brain insisted this wasn't happening, that stillness was proof of death, and proof of death meant they would stop soon.

They didn't stop.

The darkness was total. Not the darkness of a shuttered room, where eyes adjust and gray shapes eventually bloom out of nothing. This black pressed on her open eyes like thumbs. She couldn't tell whether her eyelids were up or down. When she squeezed them shut, sparks bloomed behind them—phantom light, the brain refusing to accept the absence.

Above her, the shovels worked. Then, gradually, the rhythm changed—the loose patter of falling dirt giving way to deeper, heavier impacts as the grave filled—and then, at last, silence. The worst sound yet.

Because that was when the weight arrived.

Not all at once. It settled, the way snow settles on a roof, the whole mass of it finding the lid and leaning in. The wood groaned—a long, low complaint of fibers straining—and directly over her face, along a seam in the planks, a thread of dust sifted down, fine as flour, coating her lips. She tried to do the arithmetic. Six feet. She'd heard that phrase her whole life and never once understood it. Six feet was a hill. A hill was sitting on her chest.

The box had been built to her measurements. When she lifted her arms, her knuckles scraped wood on both sides at once. To turn her head, she had to roll her cheek against the satin lining. The air was already spent—warm, thick, tasting of varnish and glue and, seeping cold through the joints, fresh-cut earth.

The panic started in her sternum and detonated outward.

She screamed. The scream filled the box and went nowhere; the dirt drank it whole. She screamed until her throat tore raw and the sound never traveled farther than the lid, eighteen inches above her mouth.

So she clawed.

There wasn't room to swing her arms—she had to fold her elbows in, wrists crossing, and drive her nails up into the underside of the lid. Wood. Solid, unbroken wood. She dragged her fingers across the grain anyway, hooked them under a knot, and pulled down with everything she had while her heels hammered the foot of the box. Nothing moved. Of course nothing moved. Above her knuckles sat two inches of air, and above *that* sat a ton of earth, and no one digs through a ton of earth with fingernails—but knowing changed nothing. Splinters slid beneath her nails. Her fingertips split. Blood made the wood slick and her grip skated off it, and she clawed harder, faster, half-mad, tearing at the grain, sobbing between efforts, whispering *please, please, please* to the dirt, to God, to anyone.

Each breath cost more than the last. The air went hot and metallic, her own exhalations recycled a hundred times over, and panic made her breathe faster, and breathing faster burned what remained quicker, and she knew this and could not stop.

She didn't know how long it lasted. Minutes. Hours. Time didn't move in here; it pooled.

When her arms finally gave out, they dropped like cut ropes, and she lay in the wreckage of her own strength, chest heaving, blood-tacked fingers curled against the lid an inch from her face. Somewhere overhead, the earth was settling—compacting, patient, learning her shape.

In a minute, she told herself. Just a minute. Then she'd start again.

Now it was gone entirely, swallowed by tissue that pulsed faintly with his heartbeat. The right eye was going the same way, the orbital bone beneath it buried under a knot of bruise the color of storm clouds.

He couldn't see. That was the plain truth of it. Blood from a split above his brow ran in a thin, warm line down into his working eye, and every blink smeared it across his vision like grease on glass. He could make out shapes—the other man's shoulders, the blur of gloves, the white glare of the ring apron when he stumbled. Sweat and blood mingled at his chin and dripped onto the canvas in small dark coins. Somewhere past the lights, the crowd roared for more, and he hated them for it, and he kept standing anyway.

Moreno backed him into the ropes. A jab to pry the guard apart—Delgado's arms were hanging low now, heavy as sandbags—then the right hand straight through the gap. It caught the cheekbone with a sound like a side of beef hitting concrete. Delgado's head snapped sideways. Spit and blood arced off his mouthpiece. He didn't fall. He hung there, propped on the top rope, legs doing arithmetic they couldn't finish.

It sank into Delgado's right side just beneath the ribs, and the sound it made was *wrong*—not the flat slap of glove on flesh but a deep, wet crack, like green wood snapping, like lake ice giving way underfoot. # The Bitter Cup

The drawing room had gone grey with November dusk, and Margaret had not yet lit the lamps. That was deliberate. In half-light, things were easier—both the doing and the enduring.

She poured the tea with a steady hand, the china making its small familiar click against the saucer. Edward took the cup without looking up from his newspaper, the way he had every evening for nineteen years.

"The new blend," she said. "From Whitcombe's."

He drank. She watched the line of his throat move, once, twice, and set down her own untouched cup.

For a quarter of an hour, nothing. The fire ticked. He turned a page. Then he lowered the paper and frowned at it, as though the print had begun to swim.

"This tea," he said slowly. "It's bitter. Bitter as quinine."

"The tannin, perhaps. It's a strong leaf." Her needle moved through the embroidery hoop, in, out, unhurried.

He rubbed at his jaw. His neck seemed stiff—he rolled his head as if working out a crick—and when he tried to set the paper aside, his fingers fumbled it. A strange restlessness came over him; he shifted in his chair, stood, sat again, his face twitching at the corner of the mouth.

"Margaret. Something is—I feel most peculiar—"

A carriage rattled past in the street below, and at the sound his whole body went rigid as a plank. He rose off the chair without meaning to, arms flung wide, fists clenched hard enough that the knuckles blanched white. His back bowed backward, further than a spine ought to bend, until only his heels and the crown of his head touched the carpet. And his face—the horror of it was the face. The jaw had locked, and the corners of his mouth were drawn up and back into a wide, fixed grin, a grinning that had nothing of laughter in it, the teeth bared, the eyes staring above it in perfect, conscious terror.

His chest did not move. He could not breathe. The muscles that drew breath were seized along with all the others, and his lips, stretched in that dreadful smile, darkened to a bruised blue.

Margaret set down her embroidery and folded her hands.

The spasm broke after perhaps a minute. He collapsed, sodden and shaking, drenched in sweat, and lay gulping air like a landed fish. His eyes found hers across the room. He knew. That was the cruelty of it—strychnine never clouds the mind. He would see everything, understand everything, clear-headed to the last.

"Don't fight it, dear," she said gently. "You'll only tire yourself."

A floorboard creaked under the maid's feet two rooms away, and it was enough—the convulsion took him again, harder this time, his body snapping into that terrible arch, the grin renewed, the breath stopped. Between the fits there would be less and less of him left to recover. An hour, perhaps two. The physician would find a man dead of a seizure, of some affection of the heart, poor Mr. Ashworth, taken so suddenly.

Margaret rang the bell for fresh tea. It would not do for the household to find the pot empty.

# The Tithe

The sirens sounded at dawn, the way they always did, and the basin filled.

Not with water — Reservoir Nine hadn't held water in eleven years. It filled with people: the condemned of the weekly allocation, drawn by lottery or by debt, and below them, in the tiered stands carved from the old concrete banks, the spectators who had traded a day's calories for a seat.

Kell had fought six times. Six times he'd walked up the service ramp afterward with his chit stamped, his arms shaking, his stomach too knotted to eat the protein ration he'd killed for. He knew the choreography now. The horn. The circle. The sand — crushed brick, actually, red as old blood, which the Wardens thought was poetic.

Across the basin stood Ilsa Voss, and Kell's stomach dropped, because he knew her. Everyone in the Lower Blocks knew Ilsa Voss. She'd taught the literacy classes in the old tram depot before the curriculum was harmonized. She'd taught Kell's daughter to read.

She held a length of rebar, wrapped at one end with electrical tape for grip. He held the same — the Wardens issued identical weapons, *for fairness*, as if fairness were a thing they believed in.

"I taught her 'moon,'" Ilsa called across the forty feet of red sand. Her voice carried flat and clear. "Your girl. 'Moon' was the first word she ever read."

"I know," Kell said.

"They told me this morning. Debt default. No appeal." She rolled her shoulders. Her hands were steady. His weren't. "I'm slower than you. We both know how this goes."

"Ilsa—"

"Don't make it long." She smiled, and it was the same smile she'd used over the reading circle — patient, tired, kind. "The long ones hurt. You know that."

The horn sounded.

They circled. She feinted left — an old teacher's trick, misdirection, make the student commit — and he didn't commit, because she'd taught him that too, years ago, in a class on rhetoric: *never answer the question you're asked; answer the question beneath it.*

She came in low anyway, because she had to. The drones hovered at the rim, and a refusal to engage was scored as forfeiture, and forfeiture meant the Long Reduction — no rations at all, a slow death in the dark of a holding cell.

The rebar caught his forearm. Pain, white and simple. He turned inside her reach the way he'd turned inside six other opponents' reach, and there was no art to what he did next, no technique worth the name. The killing blow, when it came, was ugly and small: he drove the taped end of the bar up under her sternum, a short punch of an inch, maybe two, and felt the resistance give — that soft, terrible give, like a lock turning — and then he let go of the weapon entirely, because he could not be holding it when she fell.

She fell the way tired people sit down. Kneeling first. Then sideways, into the red sand.

The basin went silent — one whole held breath of forty thousand starving people — and then the chimes sounded from the Warden tower, three notes, and the dispensary gates ground open, and the stands began to move, and the moment was over. It was always over. That was the design.

Kell knelt beside her. Her eyes were still tracking him. There wasn't much time; the sweep crew would come.

"Page eleven," she whispered. Blood at the corner of her mouth. "The primer. Page eleven. Tell her the moon poem is on page eleven."

"I'll tell her," Kell said. "I'll read it to her myself."

Ilsa Voss closed her eyes. The drones descended, patient as flies, and somewhere above them a Warden's voice, bored and amplified, called the next two names.

Kell stood when they made him stand. He took his chit. Two hundred grams. He walked up the service ramp into the grey morning, and he did not look at the bread.

# Redline

The needle was past eighty when Mara took her left hand off the wheel.

Behind her, the black Charger filled half her mirror, close enough that she could see the shooter wedged half out the rear window, braced against the frame. Ahead: four lanes of Saturday traffic, a wall of bumpers and brake lights moving at speeds that suddenly felt like standing still.

She hooked her arm out the window and fired three times.

The pistol jumped. Each shot shoved the car sideways a few inches—she felt it through the wheel, the front end going light, tires whispering across the lane line. Brass casings came back through the window frame and rang off the mirror housing, off her jaw, hot little bells. Through the tunnel of her own concentration she watched one round spark off the Charger's hood and two more vanish into the city beyond it, and she had no idea where they landed, and some cold, clear part of her brain filed that away as a problem for later.

Then a minivan drifted into her lane, signaling, oblivious, and *later* became right now.

She stood on the brake and the horn together. The minivan's driver turned—mouth open, phone lit in his hand—as she swung around him with maybe a foot to spare, close enough to read the sticker on his bumper: *My kid is an honor student.* Somewhere behind her, tires screamed. Glass burst. She didn't look. Looking cost time, and time was the only currency she had left.

Weaving now. A delivery truck double-parked with its flashers on, forcing her into oncoming lanes. A taxi braking for a fare, hazards blinking like a hazard itself. A cyclist hugging the curb who turned his head and simply stopped pedaling as she blew past, his eyes very wide. Horns rose all around her, a chorus of outrage, and every horn belonged to somebody whose worst day of the year this was becoming because of her.

Her next shot went wide. She watched it happen—watched the muzzle swing a half-degree too far as the car bucked over a pothole—and the round punched through the plate-glass window of a laundromat instead of the Charger. Mannequins. Racks of shirts. People dropping flat behind counters. A woman pulled her kid down behind a newspaper box with a motion so practiced it looked rehearsed, and Mara understood, with a lurch that had nothing to do with the suspension, that this was not the first time that woman had heard gunfire.

*You did that,* said the cold, clear part of her brain. *That's yours.*

The Charger answered. Three shots, fast, professional. One tore away her side mirror in a spray of plastic. One punched through her rear window and buried itself in the headrest beside her ear, filling her hair with safety glass. And one missed her entirely, skipped off the asphalt, and smashed the windshield of a silver Civic in the adjacent lane—she saw the driver flinch, saw the crack spider across the glass in a white bloom as the man fought to keep his family's car straight.

"Sorry," Mara said, to nobody, uselessly, at seventy miles an hour.

The slide locked back. Empty. She dropped the magazine into the footwell, thumbed a fresh one off the seat, slammed it home with the heel of her hand while steering with her knees—and the whole time the Charger grew in the mirror like a planet coming closer.

Ahead, the light at Fifth turned red. And there were people in the crosswalk—a dozen of them, umbrellas and coffee cups and a stroller, ordinary people crossing an ordinary street, forty yards away and closing fast.

Brake and die. Run the light and—

She didn't decide. Later she would not be able to say she decided. The car simply threaded the gap between a bus and a hot dog cart, two wheels climbing the curb, missing the stroller by a distance she would feel in her chest for the rest of her life, and then she was through, and the intersection erupted behind her in horns and screams and the Charger's horn, long and furious, trapped behind the bus.

For three blocks, nothing followed.

Mara's hands started shaking then—fine, electric, chemical—and she realized her mouth was bone dry and her heart wasn't pounding so much as ringing, like a struck bell that wouldn't stop. In the mirror: empty street, scattered glass, a city absorbing her like a wound absorbs a splinter.

In the passenger seat, her phone buzzed. She didn't look at it. She was thinking about the woman behind the newspaper box, and how fast she'd moved, and how many other people in this city were going to learn to move like that today.

The road ahead was green for six blocks. She took them.

Brake and die. Run the light and—

# The Ledger

Every night for four months, Ray told himself the same story, and every night it sounded a little more reasonable.

His daughter, Ellie, twenty-two, killed by a man named Dale Pruitt, who blew through a red light with twice the legal limit in his blood. Six months suspended. License back within the year. Tears in court that the judge called *remorseful*. Ray sat in the gallery and watched the arithmetic of the law reduce Ellie to a statistic, a fine, a footnote.

Everything after grew from that.

The first justification was small enough to hold in one hand: *I don't want him dead. I want him afraid.* He told himself he'd only do enough damage to make the car unsafe—something that would rattle, force Dale into a shop, into fear, into the knowledge that the world had noticed him. He repeated it like a prayer. *Not death. Fear.* It helped that he never defined exactly how much damage made fear and not death. The gap between those two words was where he lived now.

Then came the second justification, the theological one: *If it happens, it happens. I'm not pulling a trigger. I'm not choosing anything. A man who drives like that is a loaded gun rolling downhill—I'm just tipping the hill.* This one felt elegant. It removed him from the scene of his own decision. He wasn't a killer; he was gravity.

Third: *He killed her already. Whatever comes to him is just the echo.* Here Ray performed the trick that made everything else possible—he moved Dale's death backward in time, so that it had technically already occurred, and whatever Ray did next was merely paperwork. Dale Pruitt was a dead man walking. Ray was just the date stamp.

By the time he knelt in Dale's driveway at two in the morning, gloves on, flashlight clenched in his teeth, he had stopped thinking of the man at all. There was no Dale. There was a vehicle, and beneath it a darkness where a wrong needed righting. He worked quickly, clumsily, doing the thing he'd rehearsed in his head until it seemed almost administrative. His hands shook. He told himself the shaking was cold.

*This is justice,* he thought, when the work was done. *This is what the courtroom wouldn't give.*

The word *justice* did the final work. Not revenge—he'd flinched away from that word weeks ago, because revenge was selfish, ugly, small. Justice was clean. Justice wore robes. He had renamed the thing until it looked respectable, and having renamed it, he could carry it.

He drove home and slept four hours, dreamless, which frightened him more than any nightmare would have.

In the morning he took his coffee to the porch and watched the street, telling himself he wanted to see fear arrive. What he saw instead was Dale Pruitt backing out of his garage at 7:40—and in the passenger seat, buckled in, kicking his feet, hugging a lunchbox shaped like a rocket, a boy. Five years old, maybe six. Dale leaned over to fix the strap of the boy's seatbelt, said something that made the kid laugh, and pulled out at exactly the speed limit, careful as a man crossing ice, because fathers of small children drive like that.

Ray stood very still on his porch.

The justifications were still there, lined up like soldiers. *He deserves it. It's an echo. You're only gravity.* But the lunchbox floated up in his mind, bright and stupid and alive, and against it every argument revealed itself for what it had been: not reasoning—anesthesia. Four months of elegant sentences built to let him sleep. None of them had ever been about justice. They were about the unbearable fact that Ellie was gone and the world had declined to make it mean anything, and he had decided that if meaning wouldn't come, he would manufacture it out of someone else's blood.

The sedan turned the corner toward the elementary school.

Ray was moving before he knew it—keys, truck, pedal to the floor, dialing 911 with one hand, babbling about an accident, a green sedan, a child, *please, please*. He caught the car two blocks from the school gates and flashed his lights and laid on the horn until Dale pulled over, confused, furious, alive.

What Ray said to him there on the shoulder of Maple Street, he never told anyone. Some accounts say a warning about brakes. Some say a confession. Dale drove straight to a shop that morning, and the mechanic found what he found, and no charges were ever filed, because no one could prove who had done what—or almost done what.

Ray lived another nineteen years. He never called it justice again. When he thought of those months at all—and he tried not to—he understood that the most dangerous lie he'd told himself wasn't *he deserves it.* It was the quieter one underneath: *this will make it mean something.*

Nothing had ever made it mean something. Nothing ever would. That was the sentence he'd been serving all along, and no one else could carry the weight of it for him—and no one else's blood could lighten it either.

The detective's hand closed on the back of his skull before he saw it coming—fingers knotting in his hair, wrenching him forward off the chair. The table rushed up to meet him.

Impact.

For a heartbeat there was nothing but white. Then the pain arrived, blooming across his forehead where bone had met laminate, sharp and hot—and behind it a deeper wrongness, the sloshing feeling of his brain having been shaken loose inside its casing. The room tilted. He was still bent over the table, cheek pressed to the cool surface, and the world had gone sideways and slow.

Sound returned in pieces. First a high, thin ringing, like a struck tuning fork lodged behind his eyes. Then, muffled through it, the detective's voice—still talking, still asking questions, though the words arrived late and slightly underwater. *Who else was there that night. Who gave you the money.* Each syllable seemed to reach him half a second after the man's lips moved.

He tried to lift his head. His neck answered sluggishly, as if the signal had to travel through molasses. When he finally raised it, the fluorescent light smeared into a long white streak, and the detective's face swam in and out of focus—two of him, then one, then two again. A thread of warmth crept down from his nose and dripped onto the table: blood, bright red against the gray laminate, absurdly vivid next to everything else's blur.

His thoughts wouldn't line up. He knew he should say nothing, knew the lawyer's name, knew to demand the phone call—but the knowledge sat just out of reach, like a word on the tip of his tongue. What remained was pure sensation: the throb keeping time with his pulse, the sour tang of adrenaline, the table's edge pressing a cold line into his ribs.

*Stay awake,* some distant part of him instructed. *Don't nod off. Don't agree to anything.*

The detective leaned in close, and even that movement seemed to take too long, like watching it through syrup.

"You still with me?" the man asked, almost gentle now.

From very far away, he heard himself mumble something. He couldn't have said what.

She had stopped trying to be quiet minutes ago. Quiet was a luxury for people who weren't running.

The forest at night was a black so complete it felt physical, wet wool pressed against her eyes. She ran with her hands out, palms slapping bark, roots hooking her ankles like fingers. Every breath tore down her throat, cold and tasting of loam and rotting leaves. Behind her—or beside her, or ahead, she no longer knew—the woods held their silence, and the silence was the worst part. Her own crashing sounded enormous, obscene: every snapped twig a flare fired into the dark, announcing her to whatever waited in it.

Then, threaded through her ragged breathing, a new sound.

A creak. Low, patient, the groan of wood under strain—a bow being drawn somewhere in the blackness. Not the long, singing draw of a storybook archer. This was shorter, mechanical, a ratcheting *click-click-click* as something cranked itself tight.

She didn't decide to move. Her body decided for her, hurling her sideways—

—and the world whistled.

It passed her right ear so close she felt it before she heard it: a seam of cold air torn open beside her skull. Then the sound caught up, a thin, needle-sharp hiss rising into a shriek, so intimate it seemed to happen *inside* her ear rather than beside it—the sound of the night itself splitting an inch from her skin. It ended in a crack like a rifle shot as the bolt buried itself in the tree she'd been about to pass. Bark exploded across her cheek, splinters stinging like hot grit, and something warm pattered her neck. Sap, she told herself. Sap, not blood.

She lay in the ferns, cheek pressed to the frozen ground, and understood two things with terrible clarity.

First: that bolt had been meant for the back of her head. She had turned at the creak, and the creak had been real, and she was alive by half a second.

Second, and worse: he had *let* her hear it. Or he hadn't cared. Either way, the message was identical—*I see you. You cannot see me.*

A crossbow took time. She knew that much from her father's old hunting stories: crank, catch, load, lever. Twenty seconds, maybe thirty, before the next one flew. She counted as she scrambled upright, clinging to the numbers like a rope, hand over hand—*four, five, six*—running blind now, directionless, deeper into the dark because any direction was better than this one.

At fifteen, the forest went quiet again. At eighteen, she heard it once more: *click. Click. Click.* Unhurried. Almost gentle.

And she finally understood the shape of the game. He wasn't chasing her at all. He was herding her—each bolt a fence post driven into the dark, walking her wherever he pleased.

Then the clicking stopped.

**The Gleaning**

The guns have finished with their argument.
Now silence, thick as wool, has claimed the field,
and smoke unwinds from the torn earth like something
slowly learning how to kneel.

The vultures come first, high and unhurried,
tracing their circles, patient as thought,
working the morning's slow arithmetic,
counting what the light has brought.

The crows descend like scattered punctuation —
black commas on the pale page of the field —
tilting one eye, then the other,
taking the measure of all that will not yield.

The flies were first of all: a green and glinting
hum, a low, businesslike hymn,
already at the ears, the lips, the wounds,
seeding the future in skin.

The sexton beetles make their small burials,
turning the fallen under, bit by bit,
while ants march off in ranks as straight as soldiers,
bearing away the crumbs of someone's kit.

And the dead are still — that is the terrible thing,
the stillness. They do not startle, do not stir
when beak and talon test them. They are finished
with marching, finished with orders, finished with war.

One man's fist keeps its hold upon a letter,
folded small, addressed in a careful hand,
a voice from home that traveled all this way
to end unread, here in no-man's-land.

At dusk the crows will lift like ash, ascending;
the beetles finish their slow, faithful art;
the grass, indifferent, green, already pushing
through the coat of a boy with yesterday's heartbeat.

Night comes without a drum, without
a single order given — only the wire
singing its thin note in the wind, the earth
at its slow work, the field alone with its quiet.

results.model_response:
# Scraps

The can turned up beneath a collapsed shelf in what used to be a bodega—dented, rust freckling the seam, but when she shook it beside her ear there was a sound. Thick. Sluggish. Alive. Beans, maybe. Half a cup of them glued to the tin like mud.

Mara hadn't eaten in four days. Not properly. There'd been boiled pine bark on day two, and yesterday a spoonful of rendered candle wax scavenged from a church, which had torn through her like glass and left her folded double on a stairwell. Her stomach had stopped growling on day three. That was the bad sign. Hunger didn't shout forever. Eventually it went quiet and started *taking*—first the fat off her frame, then the sharp edges of her mind.

She got the lid halfway up with her knife.

The growl came from the doorway.

It stood in the broken light, gray-brown, big through the chest but starved down to scaffolding, every rib legible beneath the skin. Mange had stripped its haunches raw. Its lips were peeled back in a permanent snarl over yellowed teeth, and its eyes were the worst part—not wild, exactly. *Focused.* It looked at the can the way she felt.

There was a collar buried in the matted fur of its neck, a ring of leather grown tight, tags long gone. Somebody's dog. Somebody had taught it to sit, once. Fed it from a bowl with its name printed on the side.

It came low and fast.

She swung and missed, because the dog wasn't where her eyes said it would be. Weight slammed her hip, drove her into the shelving, dust and dead insects raining down. Teeth clamped onto her forearm—not a bite yet, a *test*—and the pain was white and total. She screamed and drove her thumb at its eye, felt the socket give, smelled the old-meat stink of its breath.

They went down together. Concrete took the back of her skull and the world strobed. Then its throat was under her hand—fur, pulse, the frantic drum of it—and she squeezed with whatever was left, arms trembling, its hind legs scrabbling against her thighs, claws opening lines of fire through the fabric.

It twisted. Got her shoulder. She felt cloth part, then skin, and something in her slid past fear into a flat, cold country where there was only arithmetic: *the can, the beans, the calories. Mine.*

Her knife hand was free. Stabbing wanted distance and angle, so she reversed her grip instead and hammered the pommel down against the side of its skull. Once. Twice. Three times, until the legs quit working and the growl unraveled into a sound she would carry for the rest of her life, and then into nothing.

Silence. Dust settling. Her own breathing like a bellows.

She lay there a long moment with her fist still knotted in its fur, waiting to feel something. Guilt arrived on schedule, punctual as ever, and she noted it the way you note weather. Somewhere under the ruined shelves, a pipe dripped.

The beans were cold, half-dried, tasting mostly of tin. She ate them with her bitten, shaking hand—two fingers, then her whole mouth pressed to the rim—chasing every crumb of rust. Two hundred calories. Less. It wouldn't matter by morning and she knew it. She ate slowly anyway, making it last, and something ran down through the grime on her face. Tears or sweat. She couldn't tell anymore and didn't check.

The dog lay on its side in the light, one eye still open, holding the hole in the roof.

Mara looked at it for a long time. At the meat on its frame, such as it was. Her stomach made a sound it hadn't made in days.

She picked up her knife and crawled over, telling herself she was sorry. Meaning it. Doing it anyway.

---

Happy to adjust this if you'd like—a different point of view, a longer fight, more interiority, or a version where the character stops short at the end.
