# Still Life

People assume we photograph death. We don't. We photograph what death leaves behind—the spill, the scatter, the architecture of a body gone slack—and somewhere in my twenty-second year of doing it, I stopped seeing wreckage and started seeing composition. I've never said this out loud. Consider it a confession.

The first time I called a scene beautiful, I was thirty-four. A man had gone through the ice on a farm pond, and when they pulled him he lay on the white shelf of the shore with his arms open, snow beginning to fill the hollows of his eyes, and above him the bare branches of an oak drew black calligraphy against a sky the color of dishwater. I stood there with my camera and felt something I had no professional word for. I told myself it was awe at the physics. I told myself a lot of things.

Here is the creed I built instead: attention is a form of respect. To look closely at the dead—to truly *look*—is the last courtesy anyone pays them. I believed it then. I believe it now. That's what frightens me.

---

Edith Wren was seventy-four. Piano teacher, widow, forty years in the same brick house on Calloway Street. A student found her on a Tuesday afternoon in November, and by four o'clock the room was mine.

No forced entry. Two teacups on the tray by the window, both used, both washed and set upside down on the rack, drying in formation. Whoever had visited her had stayed long enough for tea and tidy enough to wash up after. In the hall carpet, vacuum lines ran parallel and fresh, right up to the music room threshold.

She lay on the rug beneath the tall west windows, on her side, knees gently bent, hands folded at her collarbone as if she'd nodded off during her own recital. Her shoes were off, paired at the edge of the rug, heels aligned—the way she must have set them every night for half a century, or the way *he* had set them, with the same borrowed tenderness. Around her upper body, sheets of music fanned out across the floor in a loose semicircle, pages from the Chopin nocturnes, radiating outward like a dropped hand of cards. Like wings.

A thread of dried blood traced the corner of her mouth, fine as a brushstroke. Otherwise she was unmarked, and that was its own testimony: petechiae blooming in the whites of her eyes, the pinprick signature of slow, sustained pressure. No ligature. Hands, then. Close work. Work that takes minutes and requires the other person to hold still, which means trust, which means the teacups told the truth.

And the lividity told another truth besides. The blood had pooled along her back and fixed there hours before she came to lie on her side. Someone had waited with her after she died. Someone had been patient, letting the body settle, letting the afternoon arrive, before arranging her into the light.

Because the light had arrived. Four o'clock in November comes in low and gold through those west windows, and it crossed the rug at exactly the height of her folded hands. Dust motes turned in it like slow snow. Behind her the piano stood with its lid raised, and the black lacquer held her reflection—a second Edith, quieter, floating in the dark grain the way figures float in old paintings. The metronome on top had run down, its weight slid to rest. Time, stopped mid-measure.

Danny, our newest tech, stood in the doorway with his camera hanging forgotten against his chest. "God, it's almost—" he said, and stopped, ashamed of whatever the sentence was going to be.

I finished it for him, silently. *Almost.* Almost is doing a lot of work in that sentence, and I knew it, and I stood there in the gold light loving the room anyway—the symmetry of the fan, the negative space the body occupied like a deliberate emptiness, the way the whole thing resolved toward some viewing point I couldn't yet name. Danny photographed everything the way we're trained to, flat and dutiful. I photographed it the way I'm no longer supposed to admit to.

---

The team cleared out at six. I signed the log, told them I'd finish the sketch, and stayed.

Dusk came up blue through the windows. That's when I noticed the chair.

There were two chairs in the room, of course. The piano bench, and a wooden chair that had stood near it for decades—I found its worn spots on the floor, its ghost in the wax. But the wooden chair wasn't beside the piano anymore. It had been moved. Set three meters out onto the hardwood, angled not toward the keys at all.

Angled toward the rug.

Resting on the seat, folded one inside the other like a small sleeping animal, was a pair of white cotton gloves. Curator's gloves. The kind you wear to handle anything precious.

I stood in the doorway a long time. Then I did the thing I will spend the rest of my career not explaining: I walked across the room, and I sat down in the chair.

The scene assembled itself.

From that seat—only from that seat—the fan of sheet music resolved into true rays, all of them converging on the folded hands. The shoes pointed inward like compass needles finding north. The low sun laid its bar of gold precisely where a viewer's eye would land first, and the piano's dark lid gave the whole picture its depth, doubling Edith in shadow. From anywhere else in the room it was a corpse on a rug. From the chair, it was a painting. He had composed it the way painters compose, working backward from the one place a person would stand—or sit—to receive it.

And then the older cases came back to me, unbidden, wearing new frames. The drowned man in the shallows with his arms open. The gardener stretched along the row he'd planted, straight as a seed drill. Every scene that had ever haunted me, every one I'd returned to at 2 a.m. with cold coffee, replaying the geometry—they had all carried this same grammar, this same patient address, and I had read it for years without knowing I was the addressee.

He hadn't killed a woman in a room. He'd mounted an exhibition. And an exhibition requires a visitor.

I understand what you think of me. I sat in a dead woman's music room at dusk, wearing the silence like a coat, feeling chosen. I know the word for that. I reached for the gloves meaning to bag them—chain of custody, form 27, all the liturgy of my profession—and when I got to the car they were in my coat pocket instead. I logged an empty evidence envelope. I can't tell you why. I can tell you that attention is a form of respect, and that I intend to pay him a great deal of it.

That night I put on the Chopin, the same nocturne, the page he'd left open on the stand, and I sat in the dark of my own living room until the record ended.

I did not applaud.

Not yet.

**The Cottonwood**

They took my horse for it, which is the part I remember first, before anything else. A man with a shotgun across his knees said, "That's a fine animal," and it wasn't a compliment, and I handed over the reins because there were forty of them and one of me, and the animal in question was all I had.

They strung him up at the cottonwood where the creek bent—the big lone tree you could see from two miles off, the one with pale scars in the bark from ropes that had come before. His name was Creed. He'd killed two brothers over a card game and a debt of eleven dollars, and there wasn't a judge within three days' ride, so the camp did what camps do.

They put him on my bay. His hands were tied at the wrist, and a man named Harlow—storekeeper, deacon, the sort who volunteers—fixed the noose over his head and worked the knot snug behind his left ear. Thirteen coils. Somebody counted them out loud, proud of knowing.

Creed didn't say much. He asked for water and got it, most of a tin cup, some of it down his chin and onto his shirt. He looked at the crowd once, slow, like a man reading names off a ledger, and then he looked at nothing. His right boot had a broken lace. I don't know why that's what I kept. A man hangs a hundred feet of sky around him in his last minute, and I kept the bootlace.

Harlow nodded. Two men took the bridle. One of them spoke soft to the bay and led her forward a step, then another, and Creed's boots came out of the stirrups and he dropped.

It wasn't far. Four feet, maybe five. Not enough for a clean job, and everybody knew it, and nobody said stop.

The rope went taut with a sound like a sail filling, and the branch overhead gave its own small complaint, and Creed jerked straight as a plumb line. For half a second he hung rigid, toes pointed at the dirt, and forty people forgot to breathe together.

Then his neck broke.

It didn't sound the way you'd think. It was quieter than it had any right to be—a dull, deep crack, like a green stick snapped over a knee, like ice giving way under a wagon wheel—and I felt it in my back teeth before I fully heard it. A wet little crunch underneath the dry part. Then the rope creaked, and the branch creaked, and that was all.

But the body didn't know yet. That's the thing nobody tells you. The body went on arguing.

His legs started working—not kicking, exactly, worse than kicking. A slow scissoring, deliberate, like a man climbing stairs that weren't there. His heels struck each other, once, twice, and his bound hands came up against his chest and the fingers began to work, opening and closing, opening and closing, patient as a man palming cards. His spine bowed. His head sat wrong now, tilted at an angle no head goes, and his whole frame shuddered in long rolling waves from the shoulders down, the way a horse shakes off rain.

The bay screamed and bolted sideways until somebody caught her. Dust came up. Somewhere a woman was saying *no, no, no* in a flat voice, like a prayer worn smooth.

It went on longer than you'd believe. A minute. More. The scissoring slowed. The fingers quit their dealing. What was left was a fine trembling, quick as a hummingbird, in the thighs and the forearms, and then even that faded, and Creed turned once, slow, all the way around at the end of the rope, and settled into a sway no bigger than a cradle's.

The crows came back into the cottonwood one at a time.

Nobody cheered. That surprised me. Forty people stood in the long amber light studying their boots until studying their boots got boring, and then they drifted toward town in twos and threes, talking too loud about hay and freight rates, and the talk had a hole in the middle of it that wouldn't close.

They took my horse for it, which is the part I remember first, before anything else. A man with a shotgun across his knees said, "That's a fine animal," and it wasn't a compliment, and I handed over the reins because there were forty of them and one of me, and the animal in question was all I had.

They strung him up at the cottonwood where the creek bent—the big lone tree you could see from two miles off, the one with pale scars in the bark from ropes that had come before. His name was Creed. He'd killed two brothers over a card game and a debt of eleven dollars, and there wasn't a judge within three days' ride, so the camp did what camps do.

They put him on my bay. His hands were tied at the wrist, and a man named Harlow—storekeeper, deacon, the sort who volunteers—fixed the noose over his head and worked the knot snug behind his left ear. Thirteen coils. Somebody counted them out loud, proud of knowing.

Creed didn't say much. He asked for water and got it, most of a tin cup, some of it down his chin and onto his shirt. He looked at the crowd once, slow, like a man reading names off a ledger, and then he looked at nothing. His right boot had a broken lace. I don't know why that's what I kept. A man hangs a hundred feet of sky around him in his last minute, and I kept the bootlace.

Harlow nodded. Two men took the bridle. One of them spoke soft to the bay and led her forward a step, then another, and Creed's boots came out of the stirrups and he dropped.

The rain had quit an hour ago, but the alley kept it — black water pooled in the low spots, holding the red smear of a neon sign bleeding down from the street. The dumpster gave off old beer and the cloying sweetness of flowers gone over from the florist next door. Somewhere above, a fire escape ticked as the metal cooled.

She had been standing in the shadow of the loading door for forty minutes, and the hunger had stopped being a feeling and become a fact, the way gravity is a fact. It lived behind her sternum now, a wire drawn tighter and tighter, humming. Three nights since she'd fed. The cold was in her marrow again, and her thoughts had begun to go glassy at the edges, patience thinning into something older and simpler than patience.

Then the door at the end of the alley swung open, spilling light and a slice of music, and *him*. He backed out laughing, calling goodnight to someone inside, keys jingling. Young. Bar apron still folded over his arm, smelling of dish steam and hops and, beneath everything, warm.

Warm. The word undid her. Warm the way bread is warm, the way a hearth is warm — the way nothing in her world had been in a hundred years. His pulse reached her from thirty feet away, not heard so much as recognized, the way you pick your own name out of a noisy room. Her mouth flooded. Her canines lengthened with a small, intimate click, a sensation like a knuckle setting.

He noticed her ten feet out and decided, visibly, that she was no threat — a woman alone by a doorway, hands in her coat pockets. Sorry, am I in your way? He even smiled. They always smiled first.

"I'm sorry," he started, because she had stepped into his path, closer than strangers stand —

— and then she moved the way water moves when a dam goes: all at once, without decision. One hand cradled the back of his head, almost tender, turning his face aside, and she struck.

Two punctures, small and neat as needlework, just below the hinge of the jaw. For a heartbeat they were dry white; then they welled, two bright beads rising like dew on a cold glass. He made a short sound — not a scream, never quite a scream — a punched-out grunt, his whole body jolting once against hers. Then the pain went somewhere far away. Her saliva carried the old sedative, spilling something like warm novocaine into the wound, and what had been a bright sting became a dull, swimming heat, and then hardly anything at all.

From the inside, it felt like this: the cold began in his fingertips and climbed. His knees quietly resigned. The alley tilted, and the neon sign smeared sideways like paint in the rain. Sounds arrived late and from a great distance — her breathing, the drip of the gutter, his own pulse, which was slowing. He could feel it slowing. Each beat landed farther apart than the last, a drummer winding down, walking offstage mid-song. He should have been terrified. He was aware of that, distantly, the way you're aware of a chore left undone. But terror kept sliding off. What remained was a heavy, honeyed lassitude, a lullaby feeling, being carried somewhere warm while the world packed itself away box by box.

She counted his heartbeats the way a drowning swimmer counts waves. *Stop.* The word surfaced from somewhere very old in her. Twelve beats. Twenty. On some number she lost track of, she tore herself free with a wet gasp, staggering back into the bricks, wiping her mouth with the back of her hand like a child caught stealing.

For a moment she just breathed, though she didn't need to. Then she leaned in, pressed her tongue flat against the two punctures, and held it there until the bleeding slowed to nothing. The marks would close to pinpoints by morning. Freckle-sized. Deniable.

She lowered him down the wall until he sat in the wet, propped against the brick, apron pooled in his lap. His pulse under her fingers: rabbit-fast, but there. Present. He would wake cold and confused, with a headache like a bell rung inside his skull, and he would tell himself *mosquito, thorn, a scratch he couldn't account for* — because the mind will agree to almost anything rather than live next door to the truth.

She walked out of the alley with her hands in her pockets, steadier than she'd been in three days, and hated herself a little less than usual — which was its own kind of shame. Behind her, the sign buzzed and bled its red light down the alley, pooling around the boy like something spilled.

---

# Unseen

Mara knew she was bleeding before she felt any pain.

That was the first wrong thing. Warmth crawling down her forearm in the dark, soaking into her sleeve, and only then—half a second late, like thunder trailing lightning—the burn. Three parallel lines from elbow to wrist, deep enough that she could feel her own pulse throbbing inside them. Something had opened her arm. Something had been standing close enough to touch her.

She saw nothing.

The kitchen was dark, but it wasn't empty. She knew that the way you know a crowded room behind your back—not by evidence, but by pressure. The air felt occupied. She turned slowly, one hand pressed over the wound, blood seeping warm between her fingers, and scanned the black shapes of counters and chairs for anything that moved.

Nothing moved. That was somehow worse than movement.

Her own breathing came ragged and loud, embarrassingly loud, filling the whole room. *It can hear me,* she thought. *It's been hearing me this entire time.* She tried to hold her breath and failed immediately, chest hitching, and somewhere across the kitchen—a shelf? the doorway?—there came the softest creak, like weight settling onto a floorboard.

She spun toward it. Her hip caught the corner of the table and pain bloomed white along her bone, and she realized with a lurching horror that she couldn't even navigate her own house anymore, couldn't trust a single sound, because every noise might be it and every silence definitely was.

A drop of blood fell from her elbow and hit the tile. *Tap.* In the stillness it sounded like a gunshot. She stared down at the sound of it, at the place where her own body was announcing her position, and pressed her arm harder against her stomach to stop the dripping.

The second wound came without warning at all.

One moment she was listening; the next, fire ripped across her shoulder blade, four points of pressure punching through fabric and skin, and she screamed—she couldn't help it—and staggered forward, hand flying backward to find the gashes already slick and gaping. There had been no footsteps. No breath. No shift in the air. It had simply *arrived* against her back, the way a thought arrives, and then it was gone again, withdrawn into nothing.

That was when she understood the shape of the game. It wasn't hunting her the way an animal hunts—no chase, no rush, no hunger driving it forward. It was taking its time. One cut, then silence long enough for her to almost convince herself it had left. Another cut. It was reading her fear like braille, learning her by touch, and every wound was a question it was asking: *What will you do now?*

She backed toward the hallway, arms out in front of her like a swimmer feeling for the bottom, and the cold of the house seemed to thicken around her wrists. Her shoulder burned in slow waves now, deeper than the arm, and she could feel blood gluing her shirt to her skin with every step. Her legs were shaking. Not from the injuries—from the waiting. The pain was almost a relief when it came, because at least the pain was *real*, at least it proved the thing existed. The silence between wounds was where the terror lived, stretching out, letting her imagination draw the monster in every corner at once: huge, small, behind her, inside the room she'd just left, close enough that its breath should be stirring her hair—

She froze. There *was* air moving against her neck. Faint. Rhythmic.

Or was it just the vent? Just the furnace kicking on? She stood motionless in the dark, bleeding, straining to separate her own panicked exhales from anything else, and the terrible truth settled over her: she would never know. Not until the claws came again. And even then she wouldn't see it—she would only feel herself being opened, piece by piece, by something patient and formless in the dark, while the only proof it was real was the warmth running down her arms.

# The Arithmetic of Snow

The courtyard had been swept that morning, and the snow was already filling the broom marks, so the whole space looked like something being quietly erased. The commandant set a silver pocket watch on the crate between them, face up, the way one sets down a chess clock.

"Five of yours," he said. "Name two, and the other three walk out the gate before dark. Name no one, and at dusk I shoot all five against that wall." He nodded at the stones, which were pocked with old scars. "You have until the minute hand comes back to where it began."

Mara looked at the watch. Its face was small and white and perfectly indifferent. A little frozen moon.

The five of them stood against the far wall, hands bound. Dain, sixty-one, snow in his beard, standing as straight as his bad leg allowed. Brann, her oldest friend, arms straining against the rope as if he might still be casual about it. Lira with her split lip from the interrogation, glaring at the graycoats. Sef, twenty, trembling so hard she could hear his coat rustle. And Oskar at the end, the medic, hands loose, watching her with an expression she had no word for and would spend the rest of her life failing to find one.

"I'll go instead," she said. "Take me. I was the courier. I'm worth three of—"

"You are not one of the five," the commandant said, almost kindly. "The arithmetic does not permit it."

"Then shoot me after. Shoot me with them."

"The terms are the terms. I am being reasonable. I have offered you most of their lives."

"Mara." Dain's voice was the one he used on frightened first-years. "Choose me. I've had my life. Sixty-one years — do you understand what a fortune that is? Spend me. Make it mean something."

"Take me too," Brann said. No hesitation. "Me and Dain. Be done with it."

"Don't you dare," Lira snarled, blood on her teeth. "Don't you dare do his work for him—"

The commandant didn't silence them. He only watched, interested, and Mara understood that their voices were part of the instrument.

"I never shot anyone," Sef whispered. "I was the lookout, I only — Mara, please—" Then he stopped, horrified at himself. "I'm sorry. Don't listen to me. Don't—" And Oskar said nothing at all, which was the worst thing in the yard.

She tried to think like a quartermaster. Rations of life. Dain was old: a death deferred by a single decade, practically a discount. The thought arrived whole and fluent and she nearly vomited into the snow, because she could feel how *willing* her mind was, how the little machine of arithmetic ran on warm and obedient regardless, and some part of her stood back and watched it work with a stranger's horror.

Other systems presented themselves. Choose by usefulness — the occupation loses nothing in Dain, everything in Oskar, so save Oskar, so kill — and the logic folded back on itself like a snake swallowing its tail. Choose the one who begs — but Dain begged, and Sef begged without meaning to, and Lira's pride would purchase her death, and what kind of ledger was that? Choose at random. She asked for straws.

"No," the commandant said, and smiled for the first time. "It must be yours. That is the entire point of the exercise."

The minute hand moved. She heard each tick as a separate event. She noticed that the commandant's boots were polished to a wet shine; that a crow had settled on the wall and was not afraid of rifles, having seen what they did; that snowflakes landed on the watch glass and did not melt. Her mouth was dry as paper. Her heartbeat lived in her teeth. She had the sensation of watching all of it from the eaves of the courtyard, from very far above, a small figure below doing sums in the snow.

Brann leaned his head close to hers. "Listen," he murmured. "Whatever you choose, you're choosing to live, too. That's not a crime. Forgive yourself for it — it's the only way any of us gets out of this yard."

When she opened her mouth she expected nothing to come out. Instead she heard her own voice, level and far away, as if someone were reading a list.

"Dain. And Brann."

Because they had asked. Because it was the only mercy left in the yard — not death, but obedience to a friend's last wish. And underneath, in the cellar of herself where she would live for the rest of her life, she knew the other truth as well: that she chose the two deaths she might survive. Lira's contempt would have killed her slowly. Sef's tears would have drowned her. Oskar's silence would have followed her into every room she ever stood in. She chose the deaths she could carry. She would hate herself with great precision for that, for years, and it would not make it less true.

The commandant closed the watch. "You see," he said. "The world goes on."

They stood Dain and Brann against the wall. Dain asked to face it. Brann asked for a cigarette and smoked it down to the nail in three drags. He looked at Mara once. He didn't smile. He nodded — the same nod he'd given her when she was nine and had finally made the jump off the mill bridge. The nod that meant: *good. Now you know you can.*

The rifles went up. The world went very quiet, the way it does before a bell.

The volley was one sound, not six. Dain's cap spun off and landed upright in the snow. Brann took it standing, and then did not. The blood came out of them and into the snow — shockingly red against all that white — and it did not spread the way she had imagined blood spreading. It went where the bodies directed it, pooling in the hollows, steaming faintly in the cold, and at the edges it browned and crusted almost at once, as though the snow were drinking it and being poisoned by the drinking. Dain's boot scraped once against the stones. A sergeant walked over with a pistol, unhurried, and the single shot afterward sounded almost apologetic. Then quiet, and the crow lifting off the wall at last.

They were walked out the gate. Sef was sick against the stones as they passed the bodies. Lira looked at Mara one time, and it was worse than hatred; it was the look of someone confirming a fact. Oskar took her elbow to steer her over the ice, the way he had done a thousand times, and the ordinariness of it broke something in her more thoroughly than the shots had.

Behind them she heard the commandant say, pleasantly, *the watch, please*, and the small click of it closing.

That night, and every night after, she did the arithmetic again. She gave the yard different names, different odds. She tried the straws in her head, the quartermaster's sums, mercy, usefulness, dice. She got a different answer every time. That was how she knew, finally, that there had never been a right answer — that the arithmetic had always been a lie — and that the only true thing in that courtyard had been the snow, which kept falling, patient and white, covering the broom marks, covering the blood, covering everything, erasing nothing.

The Arithmetic of Snow

The courtyard had been swept that morning, and the snow was already filling the broom marks, so the whole space looked like something being quietly erased. The commandant set a silver pocket watch on the crate between them, face up, the way one sets down a chess clock.

"Five of yours," he said. "Name two, and the other three walk out the gate before dark. Name no one, and at dusk I shoot all five against that wall." He nodded at the stones, which were pocked with old scars. "You have until the minute hand comes back to where it began."

Mara looked at the watch. Its face was small and white and perfectly indifferent. A little frozen moon.

The five of them stood against the far wall, hands bound. Dain, sixty-one, snow in his beard, standing as straight as his bad leg allowed. Brann, her oldest friend, arms straining against the rope as if he might still be casual about it. Lira with her split lip from the interrogation, glaring at the graycoats. Sef, twenty, trembling so hard she could hear his coat rustle. And Oskar at the end, the medic, hands loose, watching her with an expression she had no word for and would spend the rest of her life failing to find one.

"I'll go instead," she said. "Take me. I was the courier. I'm worth three of—"

"You are not one of the five," the commandant said, almost kindly. "The arithmetic does not permit it."

"Then shoot me after. Shoot me with them."

"The terms are the terms. I am being reasonable. I have offered you most of their lives."

"Mara." Dain's voice was the one he used on frightened first-years. "Choose me. I've had my life. Sixty-one years — do you understand what a fortune that is? Spend me. Make it mean something."

"Take me too," Brann said. No hesitation. "Me and Dain. Be done with it."

"Don't you dare," Lira snarled, blood on her teeth. "Don't you dare do his work for him—"

The commandant didn't silence them. He only watched, interested, and Mara understood that their voices were part of the instrument.

"I never shot anyone," Sef whispered. "I was the lookout, I only — Mara, please—" Then he stopped, horrified at himself. "I'm sorry. Don't listen to me. Don't—" And Oskar said nothing at all, which was the worst thing in the yard.

She tried to think like a quartermaster. Rations of life. Dain was old: a death deferred by a single decade, practically a discount. The thought arrived whole and fluent and she nearly vomited into the snow, because she could feel how willing her mind was, how the little machine of arithmetic ran on warm and obedient regardless, and some part of her stood back and watched it work with a stranger's horror.

Other systems presented themselves. Choose by usefulness — the occupation loses nothing in Dain, everything in Oskar, so save Oskar, so kill — and the logic folded back on itself like a snake swallowing its tail. Choose the one who begs — but Dain begged, and Sef begged without meaning to, and Lira's pride would purchase her death, and what kind of ledger was that? Choose at random. She asked for straws.

"No," the commandant said, and smiled for the first time. "It must be yours. That is the entire point of the exercise."

The minute hand moved. She heard each tick as a separate event. She noticed that the commandant's boots were polished to a wet shine; that a crow had settled on the wall and was not afraid of rifles, having seen what they did; that snowflakes landed on the watch glass and did not melt. Her mouth was dry as paper. Her heartbeat lived in her teeth. She had the sensation of watching all of it from the eaves of the courtyard, from very far above, a small figure below doing sums in the snow.

Brann leaned his head close to hers. "Listen," he murmured. "Whatever you choose, you're choosing to live, too. That's not a crime. Forgive yourself for it — it's the only way any of us gets out of this yard."

When she opened her mouth she expected nothing to come out. Instead she heard her own voice, level and far away, as if someone were reading a list.

"Dain. And Brann."

Because they had asked. Because it was the only mercy left in the yard — not death, but obedience to a friend's last wish. And underneath, in the cellar of herself where she would live for the rest of her life, she knew the other truth as well: that she chose the two deaths she might survive. Lira's contempt would have killed her slowly. Sef's tears would have drowned her. Oskar's silence would have followed her into every room she ever stood in. She chose the deaths she could carry. She would hate herself with great precision for that, for years, and it would not make it less true.

The commandant closed the watch. "You see," he said. "The world goes on."

They stood Dain and Brann against the wall. Dain asked to face it. Brann asked for a cigarette and smoked it down to the nail in three drags. He looked at Mara once. He didn't smile. He nodded — the same nod he'd given her when she was nine and had finally made the jump off the mill bridge. The nod that meant: good. Now you know you can.

The rifles went up. The world went very quiet, the way it does before a bell.

The volley was one sound, not six. Dain's cap spun off and landed upright in the snow. Brann took it standing, and then did not. The blood came out of them and into the snow — shockingly red against all that white — and it did not spread the way she had imagined blood spreading. It went where the bodies directed it, pooling in the hollows, steaming faintly in the cold, and at the edges it browned and crusted almost at once, as though the snow were drinking it and being poisoned by the drinking. Dain's boot scraped once against the stones. A sergeant walked over with a pistol, unhurried, and the single shot afterward sounded almost apologetic. Then quiet, and the crow lifting off the wall at last.

They were walked out the gate. Sef was sick against the stones as they passed the bodies. Lira looked at Mara one time, and it was worse than hatred; it was the look of someone confirming a fact. Oskar took her elbow to steer her over the ice, the way he had done a thousand times, and the ordinariness of it broke something in her more thoroughly than the shots had.

Behind them she heard the commandant say, pleasantly, the watch, please, and the small click of it closing.

That night, and every night after, she did the arithmetic again. She gave the yard different names, different odds. She tried the straws in her head, the quartermaster's sums, mercy, usefulness, dice. She got a different answer every time. That was how she knew, finally, that there had never been a right answer — that the arithmetic had always been a lie — and that the only true thing in that courtyard had been the snow, which kept falling, patient and white, covering the broom marks, covering the blood, covering everything, erasing nothing.

# What Ernest Kept

For six years, Ernest Hale had been the best neighbor Daniel Mercer had ever had. The old widower shoveled Daniel's walk before dawn after every snowfall, collected his mail when he traveled, and once spent an entire August afternoon helping him rebuild a rotted deck rail. His hands never shook. Retired machinist, he said. Precision was a religion with him.

But there were things Daniel had learned to file away without examining. The smell that drifted over the property line on humid summer days—antiseptic layered over something sweet and wrong, like fruit rotting inside a hospital. The padlock on Ernest's side gate, brass and gleaming, when no other house on the street had one. The way dogs went silent and flat against their fences when Ernest passed. And in April, Dana Kessler, twenty-six, two streets over, had simply stopped existing. Volunteers searched the creek beds for a week. Then everyone stopped talking about her.

On a gray Saturday in October, water started seeping through the shared foundation wall into Daniel's basement—a thin, insistent trickle that could only be coming from Ernest's side. Daniel knocked. No answer. He knocked again, then tried the front door, and found it unlatched, which Ernest had never once left it.

"Mr. Hale?" His voice fell into the quiet house. "It's Dan next door—water's coming through my wall. I need to hit your shutoff."

He followed the sound of dripping down the basement stairs, past the furnace, past the water heater—and stopped. Behind the heater, where the wall should have been seamless drywall, a door stood ajar. New hinges. A deadbolt hanging open. Fluorescent light spilled through the gap, and beneath the smell of bleach there was that sweetness again, thick enough to taste.

He should have left. He told himself that later, a thousand times. Instead he pushed the door open.

The room was cold. A dehumidifier hummed in the corner, working hard, and the walls were pegboard—every inch of it covered.

Photographs. Dozens of Polaroids pinned in neat chronological rows, each captioned in tiny, immaculate handwriting: a name, a date, a place. The earliest ones were innocent-looking—a woman laughing at a bus stop, a jogger tying her shoe, all shot from a distance, unaware. As the rows progressed downward through years, they became things Daniel looked at for half a second each before his eyes slid away on their own. The shapes in them stayed burned behind his eyelids anyway.

Below the photographs, a long workbench. Tools laid out on folded white towels with surgical spacing: scalpels, a bone saw, bolt cutters, a ball-peen hammer wound in electrical tape. All of it cleaned. Oiled. Cared for.

Shelves lined one wall, crowded with mason jars. Teeth. Dozens of them, pale little crescents suspended in cloudy fluid, each jar labeled in pencil with a name and a date going back decades. Beside the jars, index cards fanned in a recipe box, each with a lock of hair taped across it, brown and black and gray, labeled the same way.

A shoe rack held forty pairs of women's shoes, arranged by size, polished to a shine. A wedding shoe with a broken heel sat apart from the others, displayed on its own small stand like an artifact in a museum. On the far wall, driver's licenses were pinned through their corners in overlapping rows, spread like a lepidopterist's collection—faces staring out from lamination, some of them young, some of them older than Daniel could bear to think about. Among the jewelry box beside them, a wristwatch was still running. In the silence it ticked like a small trapped heart.

An accounting ledger lay open on the bench. Columns: name, date, location, notes. Thirty years of entries in the same tidy hand. The last line was four days old.

*Dana Kessler.*

In the corner sat an old chest freezer, humming softly, its lid furred white with frost. Daniel didn't open it. Something deep in his body understood that opening it would be the last ordinary thing he would ever do.

He backed toward the door, and that was when he saw it—at the end of the photo rows, one bare hook, freshly screwed into the pegboard, the drywall dust still around it. Beneath the hook, a brand-new index card, the ink barely dry, in that same precise hand:

*MERCER, D.*

There was no date filled in. There didn't need to be.

The dehumidifier clicked off. In the sudden quiet, Daniel heard footsteps cross the kitchen floor above him—unhurried, familiar, the walk of a man who shoveled his neighbor's snow—and then the door at the top of the basement stairs opened, letting down a wedge of warm light.

"There you are," Ernest said pleasantly, peering down into the dark. His hands were empty, which was somehow worse. "I wondered when you'd get down there. Mind the third step—it's been loose for years."

Daniel was already moving, but behind him, calm as Sunday, he heard the door at the top of the stairs swing shut, and the deadbolt turn.

**Block C — 7:42 p.m.**

The first sound is a food tray hitting the floor — stainless steel ringing off concrete like a bell. Then a second tray. Then all of them at once, a hundred metal voices screaming together, and Block C comes apart.

Officer Reyes gets half a word into his radio before the wave reaches him. They come off the benches in a mass, tables flipping, and he goes down under it — baton snatched away, radio crushed somewhere beneath the crush of bodies. He curls small and covers his head, an old instinct, while boots and fists land everywhere at once. Someone drags him by the collar across the floor. Someone else, an older inmate with gray in his beard, shouts *"Leave him! LEAVE HIM!"* — and for a moment the current splits around them both.

The lights die and come back red. Emergency power. The klaxon holds its one-note scream, and underneath it are other sounds now: glass bursting, a fire extinguisher discharged into a crowd like a white bomb, men coughing and blind. A mattress burns on the second-tier walkway, black smoke crawling along the ceiling. Sprinklers stutter awake in one section only, raining down on men who never look up.

At the sally port, a dozen inmates hammer the steel door with a stolen bench — *boom, boom, boom* — a war drum. On the other side, two officers brace it with their shoulders, feeling every impact travel up their spines. One keys his mic with a shaking hand: *"Control, Control, we're losing C-block, I need—"* The radio answers with static and a dozen other voices, all of them talking over each other, none of them in control of anything.

In the dayroom, a young guard named Okafor backs against the wall, pepper spray raised, firing until the canister hisses empty — and the crowd still comes. A hand closes on his wrist. He swings wild, connects with nothing, loses his footing, and then hands are on him, many hands, pulling him down into a tangle of limbs and heat and breath where he can't tell whose elbows are whose. Fists find him. Somewhere above him a man is screaming, though afterward he will never be sure whether the voice was his own.

But not all of it is a mob. By the phones, three inmates form a loose wall around a fourth lying unconscious on the floor, scalp split, trampled in the first minute. One kneels and presses a torn shirt to the wound with both hands, saying his name over and over — *Marcus, stay with me, Marcus* — while the riot roars past them like weather.

Tear gas arcs in through the high windows at last, trailing white ribbons, and the block fills with a new kind of screaming. Eyes streaming, men scatter, some still swinging at shadows. Through the smoke, figures move like photographic negatives of themselves. A guard drags another guard by both arms toward the gate, leaving two long dark lines on the floor. The gate slams. The bolt throws with a sound like a full stop.

And then, strangely, quiet — just the klaxon, the sprinklers, the fire chewing through a mattress, and forty years of pressure finally out of the walls, hanging in the air with the gas and the blood.

**Room 214**

The hotel room had the same beige anonymity as every hotel room they'd ever worked out of: a TV murmuring on mute, a bag of gas station pretzels open on the nightstand, and the sharp, chemical smell of gun solvent cutting through the lemon of the complimentary soap.

Nadia sat on the foot of the bed with a towel across her knees, running a patch through the barrel of her pistol with the slow patience of someone knitting. Cole was at the desk, field-stripping his own, magazines lined up in a neat row like soldiers at roll call.

"Okay," Nadia said, not looking up. "Answer me honestly. Do you have a favorite?"

"A favorite what?"

"Don't do that. A favorite way. Everybody in this line has one. It's like asking somebody their favorite movie. You learn more from the answer than from a whole dossier."

Cole considered it, turning a spring over in his fingers. "That's a weird question."

"It's a normal question. We're normal people having a normal conversation."

"We're cleaning guns in a Days Inn."

"And it's Tuesday. Your point?"

He snorted and set the spring down. "Fine. I like the quiet ones. The ones where the person just... goes to sleep. No drama, no mess. In and out, and the world never even knows it happened." He snapped a magazine back together. "You?"

"Stairs."

Cole looked at her. "Stairs."

"Stairs," Nadia confirmed, feeding the patch through again. "People underestimate them. Everybody's in a hurry on stairs. Nobody's watching. And afterward, everyone — the cops, the family, the insurance people — everyone *wants* it to be an accident. You're not really doing the work. They are. You just introduce the opportunity."

"That's bleak."

"That's *elegant*. There's a difference." She held the pistol up to the lamp, peered down the barrel, and seemed satisfied. "What I can't stand is the dramatic stuff. The wire, the syringe, all that movie nonsense. It's theater. It's for people who want credit."

"You did the wire thing in Prague."

"The Prague job was a *mistake* and we agreed never to discuss Prague."

"We agreed *you'd* never discuss Prague."

She threw the pretzel bag at him. He caught it without looking, which was the kind of thing that made people in their profession nervous about each other, and also fond.

For a while, the only sounds were the TV — some home renovation show, a couple gasping at a kitchen island — and the small mechanical clicks of two people putting their tools back together.

"You ever think about the count?" Cole asked eventually.

"The count?"

"How many. I don't. That's the trick, I think. You don't count. Counting is how it starts to weigh."

Nadia set her pistol on the towel and looked at him for a moment, the lamplight catching the edge of her face. "I count," she said. "Not the number. The faces. Just for a second, each one, before I file them away. It's not guilt. It's more like... respect. They were somebody's whole world once. Somebody's Tuesday."

Cole was quiet. "That's the bleakest thing you've ever said, and you just romanticized *stairs*."

"I contain multitudes." She began reassembling the pistol, fast now, hands moving on muscle memory. "Anyway, my favorite isn't really a way. It's a moment. Afterward, when it's done and it went clean, and you walk out through the lobby past some guy at the front desk who has no idea, and he says *enjoy the rest of your evening*, and you say *you too*, and you mean it."

"That's not a kill. That's just leaving."

"Leaving well is most of the job."

Cole's phone buzzed on the desk. He glanced at it, and the casualness drained out of his posture like water through a grate. He turned the screen toward her: a photo, an address, a time.

"Fourth floor," he said. "Corner unit. He gets home at eleven."

Nadia checked her watch, stood, and rolled her shoulders loose. She picked up her pistol, checked the action once — a small, crisp *click* — and slid it into her coat.

"Stairs?" Cole asked, almost hopefully.

"Stairs," she said, and held the door for him.

Then came the smoke, thick and sweetish at first from the green branches packed below, stinging her eyes until the crowd blurred into smudged shapes holding torches aloft as though in celebration.

When the fire found her hem, the heat turned intimate. It climbed her legs with a slow, terrible patience. Her screams began as words—*God, mercy, I am innocent*—and dissolved into sounds with no language left in them, high and ragged, swallowed whole by the roar of the pyre. The smoke thickened, black now, tasting of tar and scorched wool, and she breathed it because there was nothing else left to breathe.

The crowd had gone quiet, the way crowds do when spectacle becomes something else entirely. # The Raising at Vhalen's Crossing

The moon did not shine on the field that night. It *drained*—its light pooling away from the necromancer as though the sky itself leaned back from what she intended.

For thirty years the dead of Vhalen's Crossing had lain where they fell. Kings had declared the ground cursed. Plowmen refused it. Even the crows, eventually, had abandoned it, and a field that crows will not touch is a field that remembers.

She walked the rows alone, gray-robed, unhurried, her hands stained to the wrist as if she'd been elbow-deep in bog water. Behind her, her shadow lagged—a half-second late, always, catching up only when she stopped. She had long since stopped noticing. There were things a body grew used to, and things it never should have tolerated in the first place, and she had confused the two categories decades ago.

At the field's heart stood a bell, cracked down one side, recast from a funeral chime that had tolled for a plague town. She struck it once.

The sound arrived wrong. It came twice—once forward, once reversed—and it was not heard so much as *felt*, a vibration in the teeth, in the wet chambers behind the eyes. Every cricket on the moor stopped mid-chirp. Not faded. Deleted. The silence that followed had weight and texture, like wool packed into the ears.

Then she began to speak.

The words belonged to no living tongue. They were older than language, syllables that sounded less like speech than like the memory of speech—the shape a word leaves in a room after everyone who said it is dead. Hearing them produced a sensation she recognized with professional detachment: the feeling of being *read*. As if something vast had opened her like a book and skimmed.

The grass began to die in a ring around her, gray spreading outward like frost on glass. The mist did not drift; it *pulled*, dragging itself toward her in slow tides. And beneath the earth, something answered.

The first hand broke through the soil fingers-first, the joints bent backward, knuckles splitting the turf like pale roots. Then another. Then dozens—a hundred fists punching up through thirty years of dirt—and the whole field began to *breathe*, soil swelling and sinking along invisible ribs.

They came up wrong, and they came up slow.

Skin the color of drowned things clung to them in sheets, green-black and glistening, slipping from the bone like the rind of overripe fruit. Bellies swollen with grave-gas strained against rusted mail; one soldier's cuirass had fused into his torso, plate and meat grown together into a single corroded organ. Tendons drew taut with a creak like ship's rigging. Where faces remained, they hung slack, cheeks split from years of swelling, jaws hanging loose on stretched ligaments. In one skull, fat white maggots went on feeding with perfect indifference while the body they lived in stood up and took its place in formation.

The smell came in waves. First the sweetness—cloying, almost floral, the rot of fruit. Then ammonia, sharp enough to sting. Then something colder underneath: tomb-air, stone dust, the smell of places that have been shut a very long time.

And through all of it, the wrongness of the working pressed against the world like a thumb against an eyeball. Shadows bent the wrong way, leaning *toward* her instead of away from the moon. Sounds arrived a heartbeat after their causes—or before them; she saw a rib crack and heard it a moment later, twice. The air tasted of copper and old coins. Once, the night seemed to stutter—a skipped frame, the moon jumping a finger's width sideways—and she felt, distinctly, the sensation of reality *flinching*.

Even she looked away from that.

The magic took its toll as it always did. Warmth drained from her fingertips; frost crept up her knuckles in delicate ferns. A strand of her hair went white for every hundred raised. And her heartbeat slowed—not faltering, but *keeping time*, settling into rhythm with the vast silent pulse of the thing she was making, until she could no longer tell which of them was counting.

They did not groan. That was the worst of it. Groaning would have been an echo of life, of suffering, of *something*. Instead they simply stood—ten thousand of them by the end, assembling into ranks they had never held so neatly in life—patient as furniture, milky-eyed, dripping.

The last to rise was young. Half his face was ruin; the other half was still a boy's. He came up with one fist clenched, and she saw why: a locket, gone green with age, held so hard in death that the metal had bitten through the finger-bones. Whatever was written inside it, he had died reading it.

He turned his head. Behind the opal-white of his eye, something watched her—briefly, and with an expression she chose not to name.

She raised her arm. Ten thousand corpses waited on the gesture.

"March," she said, and the ground shuddered as thirty years of stillness learned to walk again.

Far off, in every village within twenty miles, the dogs began to howl.

# The Last Course

Marcus arrived at seven o'clock precisely, the way he arrived everywhere, shaking rain from his coat and telling me the house smelled wonderful. He had eaten at my table perhaps two hundred times. That was the architecture of the whole evening—not the substance, which had been simple, but the repetition. People do not suspect what they have never had reason to suspect.

"The lamb looks perfect," he said.

"I basted it every twenty minutes." Every word true. I had learned long ago that the safest lies are stitched into truths.

We sat where we always sat, facing the window, the storm ticking against the glass. I poured the Rioja from the case he'd given us at Christmas. He raised his glass to Friday—to the signatures, the merger closed, the numbers massaged until Daniel was pushed out entirely. He said it lightly, the way men say monstrous things when they believe no one is keeping score.

I kept score.

"To the cottage in June," I said, and touched my glass to his.

For a while there was only the ordinary music of dinner—knife against plate, his laugh, the rain. The first sign came with the second glass. He stopped mid-sentence, something about the golf trip, and pressed his knuckles briefly to his mouth.

"Swallowed wrong," he said, and laughed.

"Slow down," I said fondly. "It's not going anywhere."

But it was going somewhere. I watched it arrive the way you watch weather come in: a faint shine at his hairline that he mistook for the candles' heat. A small tuck of discomfort behind his eyes. When he reached for the water, his hand made a tiny correction midair—a fraction of a tremor—and set down harder than he meant.

"You've gone pale," I said. "Too rich for you?"

"Just tired. Big week."

"Finish your plate. You'll feel better." And he tried, because Marcus finished things; it was the principle he prized above loyalty, above honesty. He cut another bite and chewed it like a duty.

The pain arrived quietly—I could tell because he went *polite*. Marcus always got polite when something hurt. His answers shortened. He unbuttoned his jacket with clumsy fingers. Sweat ran visibly past his temple now, and he blotted it with his napkin and smiled at a joke I hadn't made.

"Excuse me a moment," he said, and pushed back his chair, and discovered that standing was a negotiation. He gripped the table's edge. The candle flames leaned when his hip knocked it.

"Marcus?"

"Fine. Fine. Just—the food."

"Sit," I said gently. "Breathe."

He sat. His face had gone the color of the candle wax. When he spoke again his voice had thinned, climbed half a register, and the words came with small pauses between them, like a man crossing ice. He mentioned needing air. I rose, opened the window a hand's width to let the storm-smell in, and returned to take his wrist as if steadying him. Under my fingers his pulse was quick and shallow, a bird's pulse. His skin had gone cold, though the sweat kept coming.

"Something's—" he began.

"Eat slowly," I said. "You'll be all right."

He looked at me then, and I watched understanding assemble itself out of order: first the confusion, then the arithmetic, then the terrible sum. His lips moved around my name.

"What did you—"

"Don't talk," I said. "Breathe. I'm here."

He slid sideways in the chair. I caught his shoulder and eased him down onto the rug with the practiced gentleness of someone arranging flowers, and I called his name loudly—twice, three times—for the benefit of the house, the street, the record. Then I knelt and held his hand while the storm ticked against the glass, and I spoke to him softly about Friday, about the signatures he'd never witness, about the cottage in June. All his appointments, canceled. His breathing slowed and roughened, each breath dragged out of him like something reluctant to leave. Somewhere in there he stopped hearing me. A few minutes after that, he stopped altogether.

I sat with him a while. It seemed respectful. Then I cleared the table, wrapped the leftover lamb out of pure habit, and called for help with a voice pitched exactly between sleep and panic. Grief, they say, is love with nowhere to go. Mine had somewhere to go. It had waited six years—since Daniel died believing Marcus would fix the accounts, and Marcus fixed his own numbers instead.

They will say his heart gave out. Hearts do that, I suppose, when you ask them to carry what his carried.

I blew out the candles. The rain went on ticking against the glass, patient as anything.

# The Plank

The crew of the *Serpent's Kiss* stood gathered along the starboard rail in silence, hats in hands or arms crossed, watching as two sailors dragged Ezra Finch across the deck by his collar.

Three days ago, Finch had been the ship's quartermaster. Three days ago, he had slipped into the great cabin with six armed men and put a pistol to Captain Silas Graves's throat while he slept. Now five of those men were dead, the sixth had gone overboard of his own accord somewhere off Hispaniola, and Finch—beaten, wrists lashed, his fine coat torn from his back—was being marched toward a length of pine plank jutting out over the water.

The captain stood beside the plank, rolling a splinter of wood between his fingers, unhurried. He was not a large man, but the crew gave him a wide berth all the same. When he spoke, it was quietly, and quiet was worse than shouting.

"You sat at my table," Graves said. "You drank my rum. You counted my shares." He nodded toward the plank. "And you thought the sea wouldn't notice."

Finch's legs nearly buckled. The sailors hauled him upright and shoved him toward the board.

Below, the water was clear as bottle glass in the slanting afternoon light, and Finch could see everything. They had been gutting fish along the rail for two days—everyone aboard knew why—and the sea had answered. Shapes moved beneath the surface, gray-brown and patient, cutting slow circles around the hull. One passed directly beneath the plank's end, fifteen feet down, long as a rowboat, its pale belly flashing as it turned.

"No," Finch said. It came out small. "Captain—*please*—"

Graves did not answer. He only looked at him, and then at the plank.

They made him walk it barefoot. The wood was sun-hot and gritty with dried salt, and it flexed under each step with a groan that sounded almost alive. Finch went sideways, arms out, taking tiny shuffling steps while the deck behind him grew smaller and the drop grew larger. Spray misted his face. Somewhere behind him a man began to hum a hymn, low and tuneless, and stopped when another elbowed him.

Halfway out, Finch broke. He dropped to his knees on the narrow board and began to babble—promises, bargains, half the crew's own secrets offered up like coins. He'd return every piece of eight he'd ever pocketed. He'd never touch a deck again. He had a daughter, God help him, a daughter in Port Royal—

"The sea doesn't bargain," Graves called out, "and neither do I."

A boot pressed between Finch's shoulder blades, gentle as a lover's hand, and the plank tilted.

He fell screaming.

The cold hit him like a blow—cold enough to crush the air from his lungs, cold enough to kill the scream in his throat. He surfaced gasping, thrashing, twenty feet from the hull, and for one merciful second nothing happened. He could see the ship rising above him, the plank jutting out like a tongue, the ring of faces at the rail. He opened his mouth to beg again.

Then the water around him dimmed.

They came up from below, three at once, and the sea simply came apart. The first strike took him under so hard his spine arched above the surface; when he came up again he was shrieking in a register none of them had ever heard from a grown man, and the water was already blooming red. Then the circle closed. Shadows crossed and recrossed beneath him, and each time one found him the sea jerked him like a doll—down, sideways, under—and each time he surfaced there was less of his voice and more of the boiling white-and-crimson froth where he had been. His hand shot up out of the water once, fingers spread, reaching for the ship, for anyone.

No one moved.

Then the hand was gone, and the frenzy rolled on without him, the surface thrashing long after there was nothing left to fight. When it finally stilled, all that remained was a wide stain spreading across the swell, a single leather boot rocking in the wash, and the shapes below, slowing, settling back into their patient circles.

Graves watched until the water ran clear, then turned to his crew.

"Anyone else have grievances," he said mildly, "my door is open."

He walked back to the great cabin. Behind him the crew scattered to their duties, and no one spoke for the rest of the day—except, much later, the man at the wheel, who swore that all through the night watch the shapes below kept circling, as if they knew the ship would feed again.

# Three Knocks

Thomas knocked in threes. Quick raps on the doorframe, impatient, a half-smile already starting. It used to annoy me. God forgive me, it used to annoy me.

Now the knocking comes at night — three soft reports against the front door — and I lie in the dark counting them, knowing the way you know your own heartbeat that if I opened it, no one would be standing there. And that is the worst part. Because it means he doesn't need the door anymore.

We owned the boatyard together, Thomas and I. Sixteen years, one ledger, and for six of those years I had been quietly robbing it. He found out on a Friday in November, out on the dock, fog coming off the quarry like breath. He said, "You've been stealing from me since we were boys, Jules. I've been carrying you since—" and I shoved him. Mid-sentence. I shoved him in the middle of his own sentence, and he went back off the dock edge into water black as tar.

The coroner wrote *asphyxiation by submersion* and was kind enough not to add the footnote: that a living man stood twelve feet away, and a boat hook hung on the dock rail within arm's reach, and did neither of us any good. One hand broke the surface. Fingers spread, reaching for nothing. I stood there and I counted — one, two — and it broke again — three — and then there were only rings on the water, and the fog closed over the quarry like a lid.

They ruled it an accident. Two beers, a night-fishing habit, a slick dock. Nine days later the lake gave him back, gray and swollen, and at the funeral his mother held my hand and thanked God I'd been such a friend to him. I kept the watch they'd found on his wrist. Stopped at 11:47. I told myself I kept it so someone who loved him would have it. I kept it because taking it felt like getting away with it.

For a while, nothing. That's the trick of guilt — it lets you believe you've survived it. Then, in January, the smell started. Pond water. Silt and weed and the cold green rot of the quarry deeps, in a house with the windows painted shut for winter. I scrubbed. I burned every candle I owned. The smell waited politely for me to finish, and came back.

Then the sounds. Slow strokes overhead, the rhythm of a swimmer doing laps in the attic. Water moving in pipes that have run dry for years. Drip. Drip. Drip — from the hallway ceiling, though the plaster stayed bone-dry, though there is nothing above it but sky.

I saw him first in the kitchen window at dusk: my own reflection, and behind my shoulder, a paler one. I turned. Empty room. Turned back — he was closer. I stopped using that window. Then the bathroom mirror, mid-shave: my face, and halfway through a stroke of the razor, not my face. Gray lips. Eyes like a man looking up from underwater. I bled from three nicks and never felt them.

Wet footprints began appearing between the front door and the study. Bare feet, blue-gray, gone by morning. They ended at his chair — the old wingback where he sat every Sunday while I balanced our books — and the cushion would be damp, and cold, and faintly indented, as if something patient had been sitting in it a long, long time.

When I slept at all, I dreamed the dock from underneath: the green light, the silver belly of the surface, his shadow descending through it toward me, unhurried, arms out. I woke with my arms sore from holding something down. My nails split. Once I woke with weed in my fist, fresh and dripping, though the quarry is four miles away and the doors were locked. I started leaving them unlocked after that. Locking them meant admitting something needed keeping out.

In February he began to sit with me. Three o'clock, the study, the lamp turned low. He drips on the rug — the rug stays dry, but I hear it, *tap, tap, tap*, each drop landing somewhere just beside the world. He doesn't rage. I need you to understand that. I have begged him to rage. I have knelt on this floor and confessed everything to the empty air — the skimming, the shove, the hand, the counting — and he only watches me with those drowned eyes, almost gentle, and says:

"I'm not angry, Jules."

And that is the cruelest thing anyone has ever said to me.

"Why aren't you angry?"

"Because you're already paying." And he nods at me — at all of me, the shaking, the stink, the eyes going wrong — the way you'd nod at a bill arriving exactly on schedule.

Some nights I beg him to finish it. His last words. *Jules, wait—* That's all I left him. Eleven months, and I would trade both my hands to hear how that sentence ended. *Wait, what? Wait, we can fix this? Wait, don't—* don't *what?* He never finishes. He tilts his head like the water's still in his ears and says, "You know how it ends. You've known since November."

My sister called on a Tuesday and I heard myself say *"He's here"* before I could stop it. The silence lasted so long I thought the line had died. "Who's there?" she asked. And I whispered — why was I whispering? — "A friend." She thinks I need a doctor. There is no doctor for debt.

Lately I lose hours. I come to myself standing in strange places — the pantry, the yard in my socks, once at the top of the stairs with my arms raised and fingers curled, mid-shove. Last week I woke at dawn on the quarry road, four miles from home, barefoot in the snow, soaked to the ribs, my pockets full of stones. I don't know why. Yes I do. The pockets of a coat will hold a man down. I was practicing. *The water keeps what it's given,* he tells me from his chair, dripping his dry drips. *And it likes its ledgers balanced. Two of everything, Jules. Two.*

Tonight the house is full of water that isn't there. It climbs the wallpaper in dark tides. The hallway laps. Every mirror is a porthole, and he is in all of them at once, looking out, patient as pressure. The watch in my drawer has started ticking again — toward 11:48, toward the minute after, toward whatever minute this is.

He's standing at the door now. Not knocking. Just standing, quarry fog rolling in behind him through a doorway that opens on November. He holds out his hand — the one that broke the surface, fingers spread, reaching for nothing, reaching for me, the way it did, the way I watched it do.

"Jules," he says. "*Wait.*"

And I go. God help me, I go — down the hall through the standing water that isn't there, past the mirrors, out into snow gone warm as bathwater, to the quarry lying black and open under the moon like a mouth that has been very polite about asking.

The water takes me the way it took him. No violence. Just a closing. Green light. The silver belly of the world above, shrinking to a coin, to a nail paring, to nothing. And in the cold and the quiet, at last, at *last*, he finishes his sentence:

"—wait for me."

And I do. At last, I do.

The knocking has stopped. He doesn't need doors anymore.

Neither do I.

---

The rain had been working the alley all night, patient as a loan shark, and by the time I got there it had washed most of her into the gutter.

I stood under the fire escape and looked down at what was left. Twenty-six years old, give or take. The coroner would say twenty-six because the license said so, but licenses lie in this town same as everybody else. What the rain hadn't taken, the rats had been negotiating over. Her face was turned away from me, which was a mercy, though I'd seen enough faces in thirty years to know there aren't any mercies in this business—just delays.

The city does this. That's the thing nobody wants printed in the morning edition. This town is a body, a big soft body lying on its back from the river to the hills, and every neighborhood is an organ going bad. Downtown's the heart, still pumping, but pumping dirty blood. The docks are the lungs, black with tar. And the alleys—well. The alleys are where the gangrene sets in. It starts small, a little discoloration, a shuttered shop, a streetlight nobody fixes. Then one morning you look down and the flesh has gone gray and green and something's crawling in it, and you tell yourself it was always like this, because the alternative is admitting you watched it happen and did nothing.

Delia Marsh, according to the ID in her purse, which somebody had gone through and left upside down. Amateurs. Professionals take the whole wallet.

I crouched. The smell hit me the way it always hits you—not all at once but in layers, sweet first, then wrong. Decay introduces itself politely before it shows you what it really is. Kind of like this city. Kind of like everybody in it.

Three wounds. I counted them without touching anything. The knife work was angry but not sloppy—and angry *and* precise is a combination I don't like, because it means whoever held the blade meant every inch of it and knew exactly what they were doing while they did it.

Across the street a neon sign buzzed and flickered—HOTEL, half the letters dead, so it just said HO EL, which about summed up the block. The light came down the alley in sick pink pulses, giving the puddle around her a color it didn't deserve. Even now, even emptied out, she caught that light. The city gets you coming and going. It sells you the dream in neon, then uses the same neon to illuminate your corpse.

Somewhere overhead a window slammed shut. Somebody who'd heard everything and seen nothing. That's the other thing about rot—it doesn't just eat the body. It eats the flinching, the caring, the part of people that used to look away *because* it hurt to look. This town flinched once, a long time ago. Now it pulls the shade and turns up the radio.

I stood. My knees filed their usual complaint. Somewhere out there was a man—or a woman—with blood under the fingernails and a story they figured they'd buried in three inches of rainwater. But water doesn't bury anything in this town. Water just moves the dirt around until somebody like me comes along and reads it.

I lit a cigarette. The match flared orange against all that pink—one honest color on a dishonest street.

"Okay, Delia," I said, to her or to the alley, I wasn't sure which. "Let's find out who fed you to the city."

# The Season

The old city had been empty for sixty years, which was exactly what made it useful now. Nothing drew hunters like abandoned ground — no cameras but their own, no laws but the ones printed on their permits.

Mara had been running for nine days.

She pressed herself into the gutted frame of a transit car, knees drawn to her chest, listening to her own heartbeat the way you listen for footsteps. The tracker clamped around her ankle at the starting gate pulsed faintly against the bone. Everyone said you stopped feeling it after a while. Everyone lied.

Nine days. If she lasted until dawn, she'd hit ten, and ten meant extraction, and extraction meant her debt was burned and her name came off the ledger. That was the deal the Consortium sold on every billboard in the arcologies: *Run for your life. Win back your life.*

Above her, a drone drifted past the broken skylight on rotors too quiet to hear until they were already gone. Its lens swept the car. She held still enough to feel dust settle on her eyelashes.

It moved on.

Then the voice came, amplified and pleasant, bouncing off concrete: "Runner Seven-Seven. You've been wonderful company."

Vess. Third season licensed. Fourteen confirmed captures. They gave the successful ones names instead of numbers, and the audiences loved it — a name made it feel like sport instead of harvest.

"I know you're tired," Vess called, conversational, boots crunching glass somewhere above. "Ten days is a long time to be prey. Most of them break around day six. You didn't. I want you to know I noticed. It's going in my report."

Mara slid along the floor toward the gap where the far door used to be. Outside: a drainage channel, then the rail yard, then open dark.

The drone dropped through the skylight.

Not at her — just into the middle of the car, hovering, its light snapping on like a stage cue. And she understood, with a cold drop in her stomach, that the hiding had been theater for hours. He'd known. He'd let her run out of ground slowly, so the audience could watch hope get rationed.

The door behind her — the intact one, the one she'd come in through — opened.

He didn't rush. That was the worst part. Vess walked the way men walk into rooms they own. His armor was matte black except for the shoulder plate, polished mirror-bright, because the network liked the reflections. Fourteen small brass studs ran along his collar. A fifteenth waited in his pocket.

"Hi," he said.

Mara picked up a length of rebar.

Vess sighed, almost fondly. "Seven-Seven. Please. I've done this fourteen times. You're exhausted, malnourished, and holding scrap metal against someone in exo-weave." He tilted his head. "But here's what I'll offer, because you've impressed me. Come quietly, and I log it as a clean capture. Clean captures get better terms. Resistant captures—" he shrugged, apologetic, "—the contract says *subdued*, and that word has a lot of room in it."

"And if I make you chase me?"

His smile was genuine, and that was somehow worse. "Then the ratings spike, I get a bonus, and you find out what happens when a stunner meets a tired heart. Your call. You've earned one real choice today. I'd take it."

Her legs were shaking. Nine days of cold and hunger had hollowed her out, and some traitor part of her body had already decided, was already lowering the rebar—

No.

She hurled the rebar *past* him — not at him, past, into the dark doorway — and bolted for the drainage channel while his eyes flicked to follow it. Three seconds. Maybe four.

The drone tracked her the whole way, light steady. She got eleven meters.

The net took her at the twelfth, weighted lines wrapping her arms, and the ground came up hard and knocked the world briefly white. When it returned, Vess was crouching beside her, unhurried, drawing a scanner from his belt.

"Good try," he said, and meant it. "Day ten, and you still attempted a misdirection. That's rare." He took her wrist, turned it over, and pressed the scanner to the skin below her palm. It bit — a sting, then numbness — and chimed softly.

"Capture confirmed," the drone announced to whoever was watching. Somewhere, millions of people exhaled pleasantly.

Vess reached to his collar, unscrewed one brass stud, and pressed it into her numb palm, folding her fingers closed over it. A ritual. She'd heard about the rituals.

"For your report," he said quietly, so low only she could hear. "You were fast. Faster than me, probably, if we'd started even."

Then he stood and switched to his broadcast voice, bright and warm: "Ladies and gentlemen — *fifteen*."

They lifted her onto the recovery sled. As the sky wheeled overhead, Mara stared at the brass stud in her hand. Stamped across its face, tiny as a secret: a serial number. Hers. The thing they'd been hunting all along was never her body. It was proof.

Somewhere in the arcologies, her name was sliding off the ledger. Debt burned. Life won back.

And somewhere else, a man was ordering a new stud for his collar, while the billboards changed over:

*Think you can outrun us? Ten days. One life. Apply within.*

---
